en: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, homage to Pārśvanātha.
The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, composed by the crest-jewel of poets, the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri.
The first chapter, on the characteristics of ministers, together with the commentary composed by Śrī Bandhuṣeṇa. || 1 ||
Vivaraṇa:

[I bow to] Him whose fame, accompanied by the dances and songs of the celestial damsels of the four classes of gods, pervades the entire circle of the quarters, and who is adorned with the eightfold great miracles beginning with the sounding of divine drums.
Having bowed to Śrī Pārśvanātha, who overcame the fierce and terrible afflictions wrought by Kamaṭha,
the *Kalpapravara-vivaraṇa* shall indeed be spoken by Bandhuṣeṇa, accompanied by Padmāvatī.

Having prostrated before the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Jina Pārśva, who crushed the assault of Kamaṭha, I shall describe the ritual manual (kalpa) of Bhairava and Padmāvatī, which bestows desired fruits. 1.1.
Vivaraṇa:

“The crusher of Kamaṭha’s assault” means that which crushes the assault performed by Kamaṭha; thus, it is "the crusher of Kamaṭha’s assault. Furthermore, of what nature is he? "The Lord of the Three Worlds," the sovereign of the three realms. Who? "Pārśva-jina," the venerable Lord Jina Pārśva. Having done what? "Having prostrated," having bowed down with excellence, "I shall speak," I shall set forth.

What [is it]? "The Bhairavapadmāvatī-kalpa. She is both Bhairavī and Padmāvatī, thus Bhairavapadmāvatī; her ritual manual (kalpa) is the Bhairavapadmāvatī-kalpa—[I shall speak] that Bhairavapadmāvatī-kalpa. Of what nature is it? "Bestowing the desired fruit" (abhīṣṭaphalaprada): it bestows the fruit that is longed for, hence it is the bestower of the desired fruit. The connection [of the sentence] is: "I shall speak that which bestows the desired fruit. // 1.1 //

May that goddess Padmā, who has three eyes and the luster of red flowers, protect me—she who holds a noose, a fruit, and the gesture of granting boons in her hands, who causes elephants to be subdued, and who sits upon a lotus throne. 1.2.
Vivaraṇa:

“She whose hands hold the noose, the fruit, the gesture of granting boons, and the means for subduing elephants” (*pāśaphalavaradagajavaśakaraṇakarā*): the noose (*pāśa*), the fruit (*phala*), the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the means for subduing elephants (*gajavaśakaraṇa*)—she in whom these are present, starting from the upper left hand and so forth in sequence, is “she whose hands hold the noose, the fruit, the gesture of granting boons, and the means for subduing elephants. Furthermore, of what nature is she? “Seated upon a lotus” (*padmaviṣṭarā*): she whose seat (*viṣṭara*) is the lotus itself is “seated upon a lotus.”

Furthermore, of what nature is she? "Trilocanā": she who possesses three eyes (locanas) is Trilocanā. Furthermore, of what nature is she? "Raktapuṣpābhā": she whose radiance (ābhā)—that is, her luster—is like that of a red flower (raktapuṣpa) is Raktapuṣpābhā. Who is she? "Padmā," namely Padmāvatī by name. "Devī" means a goddess. "Māṃ"—the author of this work, the venerable Malliṣeṇācārya—"rakṣatu" means may she protect. // 1.2 //
Totalā, Tvaritā, Nityā, Tripurā, Kāmasādhinī—
these are the names of the Goddess Padmā, as well as Tripurabhairavī.
Vivaraṇa:
Totalā and the others, ending with Tripurabhairavī, are the synonymous names of the goddess Padmāvatī—they arise as such. 1.3.
[Page 2] First, the characteristics of the practitioner; then the sequence for the worship of the Goddess with all limbs complete;
thereafter, the exposition of the twelve varieties of yantras; and [the rites of] paralyzing and attracting women.

I shall now describe in due order the yantras that bring subjugation, the other signs, the subjugating herbs, and the science of Garuḍa, according to the authorities as they have been declared in the ritual manual.
Vivaraṇa:

At the beginning of the treatise, "the characteristics of the practitioner" refers to the characteristics of those who practice mantra. "Susakalīm" refers to the ritual of the complete integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*). "The sequence for the worship of the Goddess" refers to the procedure for propitiating the Goddess. "Afterwards" means immediately following the procedure for propitiating the Goddess. "The exposition of the twelve types of yantras" refers to the detailed explanation of the twelve varieties of yantras. "Stambha" refers to the section concerning the yantras for paralyzing anger and so forth. [“Aṅganākarṣaṇa” refers to the section concerning the attraction of women.]

The section on "the machine for subjugation" (*yantraṃ vaśyakaram*) refers to the chapter describing the machines for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). "The sign" (*nimittam*) refers to the chapter on signs such as mirrors and the like. "The other" (*aparam*) means another [section]. "Subjugating herbs" (*vaśyauṣadham*) refers to the chapter on herbs for subjugating women and others. "The Gāruḍa" refers to the chapter on the Gāruḍa [mantras].

"The chapters in this ritual manual" (*kalpe 'dhikārāḥ*): in whatever manner these chapters have been expounded (*nigaditāḥ*) in this ritual manual (*kalpe*), in that same manner (*tathā*) I, the venerable teacher Malliṣeṇa, shall explain (*vakṣye*) them in due order (*kramaśaḥ*). // 1.4 //
Thus, Malliṣeṇa composes this ritual manual for Queen Padmāvatī, consisting of ten chapters, composed in graceful Āryā verses, songs, and excellent meters.
*Vivaraṇa*:

Regarding the phrase “by means of ten kinds of chapters”: thus, by means of the ten types of chapters previously mentioned. Of what nature are they? “By means of charming *āryā*s, *śloka*s, songs (*gīti*), and excellent meters (*sadvṛtta*): *Lalitāryā* is that which is both charming and an *āryā*; a *śloka* is one composed of thirty-two syllables; “song” refers to the *upagīti*; and “excellent meters” refers to the twenty-six *jāti* and *vṛtta* meters. “He composes” (*viracayati*) means he arranges with particular care. Who is the author? Malliṣeṇa. What is it? A ritual manual (*kalpa*).
For whom? “Of Queen Padmāvatī,” that is, of the goddess Bhairavī-Padmāvatī. (1.5)

Having conquered the arrogance of passion, having pacified anger, and having abandoned frivolous talk, the mantra-practitioner should be devoted to the worship of the Goddess and faithful to the feet of the Jina. 1.6.
Vivaraṇa:

“One who has conquered the arrogance of Māra” (*nirjitamadanāṭopaḥ*) means one by whom the arrogance—the manifestation—of Māra has been completely conquered. “One whose anger has been pacified” (*praśamitakopaḥ*) means one by whom anger has been thoroughly calmed. “One who has abandoned idle chatter” (*vimuktavikathālāpaḥ*) means one by whom idle chatter—the talk of frivolous discourse—has been specifically released or abandoned.

“Devoted to the worship of the Goddess” means devoted to the worship—namely, the adoration—of the Goddess Padmāvatī. “Devoted to the feet of the Jina” means devoted to the lotus-feet of the illustrious Jineśvara. This “minister,” that is, a practitioner of mantra, “should be” one endowed with such qualities. (1.6)
A hero in the propitiation of mantras, far removed from evil, profound in virtue, silent, and possessing great self-respect—such a person should be a minister of mantras. (1.7)
Commentary:

"Mantrārādhana" means the propitiation of the mantra; one who is brave (*śūra*)—that is, fearless—in that regard is a "hero in the propitiation of mantras. Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is "far from evil" (*pāpavidūra*), meaning far from the performance of wicked deeds. He is "profound through his virtues" (*guṇena gambhīra*), meaning profound by virtue of possessing all [excellent] qualities. One in whom silence (*mauna*) exists is a "silent sage" (*maunī*). "Greatly conceited" (*mahābhimānī*): "great" (*mahān*) and "conceit" (*abhimāna*) together form "great conceit"; one in whom that exists is "greatly conceited. "Such a person"—a man distinguished by these qualities—"should be a counselor" (*mantrī*), a practitioner of mantras. (1.7)
One who follows the beneficial instructions of his elders, is free from sloth, has abandoned sleep, and is habituated to moderate eating— such a person shall be a worshiper of the Goddess. 1.8.
*Vivaraṇa*:

"One who has received beneficial instruction from his elders" (*gurujanahitopadeśaḥ*) means one by whom beneficial instruction has been imparted (*āhita-upadeśaḥ*) from the presence of his elders. "Free from sloth" (*gatatandraḥ*) means devoid of laziness. "Abandoned by sleep" (*nidrayā parityaktaḥ*) means free from excessive sleep. "Habituated to moderate eating" (*parimitabhojanaśīlaḥ*) means one whose habit (*śīla*) is moderate food. "He" refers to a person distinguished by such qualities. "Of the Goddess" (*devyāḥ*) refers to Padmāvatī. "A worshipper" (*ārādhakaḥ*) means a practitioner (*sādhakaḥ*). "Should be" (*syāt*) means he ought to be.

One who has conquered the passions of the sense objects, whose body is filled with joy born from the nectar of Dharma, and who is replete with the most excellent virtues—he shall be a worshipper of the Goddess. 1.9
Vivaraṇa:

“One who has conquered the objects and the passions” (*nirjitaviṣayakaṣāyaḥ*): objects (*viṣaya*) are those arising from the five senses and so forth; passions (*kaṣāya*) are anger and so forth. Objects and passions together are "objects and passions" (*viṣayakaṣāya*). He by whom these objects and passions have been conquered is "one who has conquered the objects and the passions."

Furthermore, of what nature is he? "One whose body has attained joy produced by the nectar of Dharma" (*dharmāmṛtajanitaharṣagatakāya*): Dharma itself is the nectar, thus "the nectar of Dharma" (*dharmāmṛta*). Joy produced by that is "joy produced by the nectar of Dharma" (*dharmāmṛtajanitaharṣa*). He is one whose body—his physical frame—has gone to, that is, attained, such joy; he is "one whose body has attained joy produced by the nectar of Dharma. "Filled with most weighty virtues" (*gurutaraguṇasampūrṇa*): filled with most distinguished qualities. "He would be a worshipper of the Goddess" (*sa bhaved ārādhako devyāḥ*): that person, distinguished by such qualities, would be a worshipper of the Goddess—Padmāvatī. (1.9)

Pure, serene, devoted to the guru and the gods, firm in his vows, endowed with truthfulness and compassion, skillful, clever, and capable of grasping the seed-syllables and words—such indeed should a practitioner of mantra be in this world. (1.10)
*Vivaraṇa*:

"Pure" means pure both externally and internally. "Serene" means having a gentle mind. "Devoted to the guru and the gods" means one who is devoted toward the guru and the deities. "Firm in his vows" means exceedingly steadfast in the vows he has undertaken. "Endowed with truth and compassion" means endowed with truthful speech and mercy. "Dexterous" means extremely clever. "Sharp-witted" means intelligent. "One who grasps the seed-syllables and words" refers to one in whom the apprehension of the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) and words exists; such a person is of this very kind.
‘In the world’ means in the midst of the world; ‘the practitioner’ means one who speaks mantras; ‘should be’ means he ought to be. // 1.10 //
A man in whom these qualities are not present should never, at any time, be a minister.
If, out of pride, he performs the recitation of the mantra of Śrī Phaṇiśekharā, he incurs misfortune. (1.11)
Vivaraṇa:

“Of that person who does not possess these qualities”—that is, for whichever man these qualities do not exist—“somewhere,” in any place whatsoever; “at some time,” at any time whatsoever; “he,” such a distinguished man; “a practitioner of mantra” (mantrī), one who recites mantras; “would not be,” he would not be [one]. “He,” the man; “out of pride,” by way of an arrogant disposition; “if he performs the recitation” (jāpya)—that is, the recitation of mantras—if he should perform it [then he is not a true practitioner].
"He incurs misfortune from Phaṇiśekharā" means he incurs—falls into—misfortune from Queen Padmāvatī. 1.11.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the characteristics of the minister, in the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa* composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri, the crest-jewel of poets in both languages. || 1 ||
Vivaraṇa:

"Thus" (*iti*) means in this manner. "Composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri": *Śrī* denotes one who is distinguished by glory; he is Malliṣeṇa, thus *Śrīmalliṣeṇa*. He is also a *sūri* (teacher/master), thus *Śrīmalliṣeṇasūri*. That which was composed—that is, narrated—by him, in that [work] composed by Śrīmalliṣeṇasūri. Where? In the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa*, the first chapter concerning the characteristics of the mantra-practitioner (*mantrin*) within the *mantrakalpa* of the goddess Bhairavapadmāvatī. // 1 //
The second chapter: The Section on the Totalization of the Body. || 2 ||
Having first bathed, the practitioner, wearing freshly washed red garments,
should stand in a cleansed place and perform the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkriyā*).
Vivaraṇa:

“Having bathed” means having performed the ritual ablution. “First” means beforehand. “The Mantrin” is the practitioner of mantra. “Clad in washed red garments” means wearing purified crimson clothing. “In a swept place” means in a place smeared with cow dung. “Staying” means remaining there. One should perform the “act of complete protection,” which is the rite for self-protection. // 2.1 //
Hrāṃ should be on the thumb of the left hand, hrīṃ on the index finger, hrūṃ on the middle finger, hrauṃ again on the ring finger, and hraḥ on the little finger. (2.2)
Vivaraṇa:

“*Hrāṃ* on the left thumb”—one should place the seed-syllable *hrāṃ* on the tip of the left thumb. “*Hrīṃ* on the index finger”—the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* on the tip of the index finger. “*Hrūṃ* on the middle finger”—the seed-syllable *hrūṃ* on the tip of the middle finger. “*Hrauṃ* again on the ring finger”—furthermore, subsequently, the seed-syllable *hrauṃ* on the tip of the ring finger. “And *hraḥ* on the little finger”—the seed-syllable *hraḥ* on the tip of the little finger; the word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction.

In this manner, the placement of the five seed-syllables of emptiness should be performed in successive order: hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ are the syllables for the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the tips of the fingers. 2.2.

With the five words of salutation, each preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the word for oblation (*svāhā*), and with the previously mentioned five voids (*pañcaśūnya*) placed at the beginning of the word for the Supreme Preceptor (*parameṣṭhin*). || 2.3 ||

"Protect, protect my head, face, heart, navel, and feet"—with these [mantras], the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon his own limbs every day. (2.4) [A *kulaka*].
Commentary:

"By the five words of salutation" means preceded by salutations to the Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas, and all Sādhus, consisting of these five words. Of what nature are they? "Each preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with the word *svāhā*" means individually preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word *svāhā*.

By what kind [of syllables]? "Placed specifically at the tips of the feet of the five supreme beings (pañcaparameṣṭhin)," meaning they are specifically arranged in their proper sequence at the tips of the feet of the five supreme beings. By which [syllables]? "By the previously mentioned five voids (pañcaśūnya)," meaning by the five voids in the form of *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hrauṃ*, *hraḥ*—that is, by the five *ha*-syllables. // 2.3 //

‘Head’ (*śīrṣa*) means the crown of the head; ‘face’ (*vadana*) means the mouth; ‘heart’ (*hṛdaya*) means the region of the heart; ‘navel’ (*nābhi*) means the region of the navel; ‘feet’ (*pādau*) means the two feet; ‘and’ (*ca*) is for the purpose of conjunction; ‘protect, protect’ (*rakṣa rakṣa*) are two words. In this manner, with ‘these’ aforementioned mantras, ‘the practitioner of mantras’ (*mantrī*), day by day, ‘should perform’ (*kuryāt*) ‘the placement upon his own limbs’ (*svāṅgavinyāsa*). // 2.4 //

Oṃ, homage to the Arhats; Hrāṃ, protect, protect the head, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Siddhas; Hrīṃ, protect, protect the face, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Ācāryas; Hrūṃ, protect, protect the heart, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Upādhyāyas; Hrauṃ, protect, protect the navel, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to all the holy ones in the world; Hraḥ, protect, protect the feet, svāhā! Thus is the sequence for the ritual placement upon the limbs (aṅganyāsa).

One should perform the binding of the directions by placing the *kūṭa* syllables— consisting of two, four, sixty-two, and fourteen *kalās*, joined with the nasal bindu and the final vowel— in the ten directions.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“By means of the two, four, sixth, and fourteenth *kalās*”: the two-*kalā* is the vowel *ā*; the four-*kalā* is the vowel *ī*; the sixth-*kalā* is the vowel *ū*; the fourteen-*kalā* is the vowel *au*. By means of these vowels—those consisting of two, four, six, and fourteen *kalās*—and how characterized? “Joined with the final vowel and the *bindu*”: the final vowel is the syllable *aṃ*; joined with that final vowel and the *bindu*, which is the *anusvāra*. By what? By the *kūṭas*, namely the syllables *kṣ*.

By what means? "Placed in the directions" (digvinyastaiḥ), meaning placed in the cardinal points. In which? In the directions (diśāsu). "One should perform the binding of the directions" (digbandhanaṃ kuryāt), meaning one should effect the confinement of the directions. The extraction [of the mantras] is as follows: KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢŪṂ KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ. // 2.5 //
The practitioner of mantra should visualize a golden rampart, square and very lofty,
measuring twenty cubits, [constructed] with the voids [of the vowels] conjoined with all the consonants.

*Vivaraṇa*: “Made of gold” (*hemamaya*) means consisting of gold. What? A wall (*prākāra*), that is, a fortress. Of what nature is it? “Quadrangular” (*caturasra*), meaning four-cornered. Again, of what nature? “Highly elevated” (*samuttuṅga*), meaning perfectly lofty. Furthermore, how characterized? “Twenty cubits” (*viṃśatihasta*), meaning measuring twenty cubits. “With zeros joined to all vowels” means with the letter *ha*. “The practitioner” (*mantrī*), i.e., the reciter of mantras, “should contemplate” (*cintayet*)—he should meditate upon, he should perform meditation on, a wall distinguished by such qualities. // 2.6 //
One should meditate on the form of a water-vessel even with syllables complete in all their vowels, filled with pure water and teeming with most terrifying aquatic creatures. (2.7)
Commentary:

"With all the musical notes complete" (*sarvasvarasaṃpūrṇaiḥ*). By what means? "By the *kūṭas*, [that is] by the *kṣa*-syllables. "Even" (*api*) is used for emphasis. "In the form of a moat" (*khātikākṛtim*), meaning having the shape of a trench. "One should meditate" (*dhyāyet*), one should perform meditation. Of what nature is it? "Filled with pure water" (*nirmalajalaparipūrṇām*). Again, of what nature is it? "Teeming with most terrifying aquatic creatures" (*atibhīṣaṇajalacarākīrṇām*), meaning filled with most fearsome aquatic beings such as fish, crocodiles, *makaras*, tortoises, and so forth. (2.7)
Having meditated upon himself as being burnt by the flames of the blazing syllable *oṃ* and *raṃ*, and situated within a city of fire,
he should thereafter perform his bath with this nectar-mantra.

Vivaraṇa: “Blazing with the *oṃ* and *ra* syllables” means: the blazing *oṃ* syllable and the *ra* letters; [he is] burnt by their flames—thus, "burnt by the flames of the blazing *oṃ* and *ra* syllables. What? "Himself," that is, the self (*ātmānam*). Of what nature? "Situated in front of the fire," meaning situated in the center of the circle of fire (*agnimaṇḍala*). "Having meditated" means having performed meditation. "Afterwards" means immediately following the meditation. "With this" means with the following. "With the nectar mantra" means with the mantra to be described. "Bath" means the mantra-bath. "Let him perform" means he should do it.
The mantra: Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya saṃ saṃ klīṃ klīṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ hrāṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ drāvaya drāvaya hrīṃ svāhā. This is the Amṛta-mantra.

One should meditate upon the Moon-like Lord Pārśvajina, who has been bathed on the peak of the celestial mountain of one's own head by hosts of lords of gods with the milk of the Ocean of Milk, his body purified by that water.
Vivaraṇa:

‘On the peak of the divine mountain of one’s own head’: one’s own head itself is the divine mountain—Meru; its peak is the summit; on that peak of the divine mountain of one’s own head. ‘Bathed thoroughly’: completely bathed. Who? ‘The moon-like Lord of Jinas, Pārśva. By what? ‘By the milk of the ocean of milk,’ that is, by the milk of the Milky Ocean. By whom? ‘By the hosts of the lords of gods,’ that is, by the multitudes of the celestial rulers. ‘One should contemplate oneself’: one should meditate upon the self.
‘Tajjalaśuddhagātram’: his body becomes pure by means of that bathing water. // 2.9 //
Through this meditation, elemental spirits, seizing demons, and *śākinīs* do not approach;
it swiftly removes even previously accumulated misdeeds in this very life. (2.10)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Spirits, seizing-demons, and *śākinīs*”: spirits (*bhūta*), seizing-demons (*graha*), and *śākinīs*—these are “spirits, seizing-demons, and *śākinīs*. “By this meditation”: by the meditation thus described. “They do not approach”: they are unable to effect an approach. “Even that which was previously accumulated”: even that acquired in a prior birth. What is it? “Misfortune” (*durita*), i.e., evil karma. “Swiftly indeed”: very quickly. “He removes”: he destroys. // 2.10 //
Seated in the paryanka posture with the articles of worship placed nearby,
he should apply a tilaka of excellent sandalwood paste both upon himself and upon the women of the quarters.

"Seated in the paryanka posture" means established in the cross-legged position. "Possessing articles of worship situated nearby" means having the eight kinds of ritual materials for worship placed at his own side. "The forehead mark (tilaka) of the women of the directions" refers to the tilaka—the special mark—of the brides of the eight directions, beginning with the East. "And of himself" means also of one's own self. "From fine sandalwood" means with beautiful sandalwood; "he should make" means let him apply the tilaka. // 2.11 //
I bow to her who has the Lord of Serpents as her crest-ornament, who sits upon a vast, ruddy lotus seat,
whose vehicle is the cock-serpent, who possesses a ruddy luster and a lotus-like face;
she who has three eyes and is marked by the divine fruits of the boon-granting hand, the goad, and the extended noose.
One should meditate upon Kamalāvatī, who bestows the fruit [of success] upon virtuous people engaged in recitation.
Vivaraṇa:

"She who has the Lord of Serpents as her crest-jewel" (*pannagādhipaśekharā*): the Lord of Serpents (*pannagādhipa*) is Dharaṇendra; she in whose crest (*śekhara*)—that is, the tip of the crown—is he found, she is *pannagādhipaśekharā*, her. Of what nature is she? "Seated upon a broad, red lotus" (*vipulāruṇāmbujaviṣṭarā*): she whose seat (*viṣṭara*) is a broad (*vipula*) and expansive (*vistīrṇa*) red lotus (*aruṇāmbuja*), she is *vipulāruṇāmbujaviṣṭarā*, her. Furthermore, of what nature is she? "Having the cock-serpent as her vehicle" (*kurkuṭoragavāhanām*): having the cock-serpent (*kurkuṭasarpa*) as her mount (*vāhana*).

Furthermore, of what specific qualities is she possessed? "Aruṇaprabhām": she whose radiance—her luster—is like that of vermilion; such is she. Again, of what specific qualities? "Kamalānanām": she whose face—the mouth—is like a lotus; such is she. "Tryambakām": she who possesses three eyes—three locanās; such is she.

Furthermore, of what specific qualities is she? She is "marked with the boon-granting [gesture], the goad, the extended noose, and the divine fruit" (*varadāṅkuśāyatapāśadivyaphalāṅkitā*). That is, she whose hands are marked—that is, inscribed—with these: the boon-granting gesture, the goad, the extended noose, and the divine fruit; such is she, and one should meditate upon her. Whom? One should contemplate *Kamalāvatī*, that is, Padmāvatī.

Of what specific qualities is she? She is "the bestower of fruits" (*phaladāyinī*) to "the virtuous ones" (*satām*), meaning good persons, who are "reciting," that is, performing their prayers. (2.12)
Having first understood the respective portions of both the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment, the wise person should offer the mantra; otherwise, its fruit is in vain. (2.13)

Vivaraṇa: “Having fully understood” means having correctly known. What? “The portion,” that is, the maternal portion (*mātrāṃśaka*). “Previously” means beforehand. Of whom? “Of the goal and the practitioner” (*sādhyasādhakayoḥ*); the goal is the mantra, and the practitioner is the mantrin—of these two, the goal and the practitioner. “Also” means certainly. “One should communicate the mantra” means one should provide the instruction on the mantra.

‘Prājñaḥ’ means the wise one. ‘Anyathā’ means in the absence of knowledge of the [proper] parts. ‘Tatphalam’ means the fruit of that mantra. ‘Vyartham’ means it would become useless or devoid of purpose. // 2.13 //

Having separated the names of the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment into their vowels, consonants, and anusvāras, they should be arranged sequentially according to their division into upper and lower parts. (2.14)
Vivaraṇa:

"The names of the goal and the practitioner" means the name of the *sādhya*—the mantra—and the name of the *sādhaka*—the mantrin. "The anusvāra," "the consonants"—the phonemes beginning with *ka*—"and the vowels"—the vowels beginning with *a*. "Having separated them" means having analyzed them individually. "To be placed in order" means they are to be established according to the sequence of the goal and the practitioner. How so? "By way of upper and lower division": one should place the name of the goal above and the name of the practitioner below, establishing them according to this method of division. (2.14)

The syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be counted starting from the syllable of the practitioner’s (sādhaka) own name; having excluded neuter syllables, one should divide that total by four.
Commentary:

“The syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished” (*sādhyanāmākṣaram*) means the letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). “From the syllables of the name of the practitioner” (*sādhakāhvayavarṇataḥ*) means from the letters of the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). “It should be counted” (*gaṇyam*) means one should count them. Having done what? “Having discarded the neuter vowels” (*napuṃsakaṃ parityajya*), that is, having discarded the neuter vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. “That divided by four” (*tad vedabhājitam*): one should divide that—the aggregate of the anusvāras and consonants being counted for both the one to be accomplished and the practitioner—by the Vedas, i.e., by four. (2.15)
The wise one should set aside that portion extracted from the total in sequence:
one, two, three, and four; [the results being] Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and Ari. (2.16)
Vivaraṇa:

"The quotient obtained by division" (*āyo bhāgoddharitam*) means that when the quantity consisting of the subject to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving factors (*sādhaka*) is divided by four, what remains is the quotient (*āya*). "And that" (*taṃ ca*) refers to that remaining quotient. "One should place it at the beginning" (*ādyaṃ sthāpayet*) means one should place it at the start of the row of consonants and anusvāras from which the subject to be proven has been subtracted. How? "In sequence" (*kramāt*), that is, according to the order in the row. Who? The wise person (*dhīmān*).

"Regarding the one, two, three, or four syllables [of the name]: 'Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, Ari'—when extracted once it is Siddha; when extracted twice it is Sādhya; when extracted thrice it is Susiddha; when extracted four times it is an enemy (Ari); thus it should be understood. (2.16)
The wise man should accept the *siddha* and *susiddha* [planets], but avoid the *sādhya* and the enemy [planet].
The *siddha* and *susiddha* yield fruit; the *sādhya* and the enemy are fruitless. (2.17)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“One should accept *siddha* and *susiddha*”: among the four *āyas*, the two *āyas* known as *siddha* and *susiddha* are to be accepted. “One should avoid *sādhya* and the enemy (*śatru*)”: among those *āyas*, the two *āyas* known as *sādhya* and *śatru* are to be avoided. Who? “The wise one” (*dhīmān*), that is, the intelligent person. “*Siddha* and *susiddha* are fruit-bearing”: when the two *āyas* known as *siddha* and *susiddha* are productive, the fruit of the mantra arises. “It is fruitless in *sādhya* or in the enemy”: in the two *āyas* known as *sādhya* or *śatru*, the mantra would be fruitless. (2.17)
If a *siddha* [planet] yields fruit within a few days, a *sādhya* one does so even after many days;
a *susiddha* one yields fruit instantly, whereas an *ari* [enemy] planet is the destroyer of life and wealth. (2.18)
Vivaraṇa:

"If it is accomplished" (*siddhaṃ cet*) means if the mantra is accomplished. "In a few days" (*katipayadivasaiḥ*) means in however many days. "Yielding fruit" (*phaladaṃ*) means it becomes a giver of results. "Even that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) after many days"—that is to say, subsequently, a mantra that is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) yields fruit after many days. "Immediately yielding fruit, well-accomplished" (*jhaṭiti phaladaṃ susiddhaṃ*): a well-accomplished (*susiddha*) mantra yields fruit immediately, that is, quickly.
‘The enemy who destroys life and wealth’: such an enemy brings about the destruction of one’s life and wealth through counsel. // 2.18 //
If there is an enemy [vowel] at the beginning or at the end, then one should abandon the mantra;
if there is an enemy in all three positions, there will be death or the failure of the undertaking. (2.19)
Vivaraṇa:

"If there is a *śatru* [vowel] at the beginning or the end" means that if there is a *śatru* at the beginning of the mantra or at the end of the mantra, "then one should abandon the mantra," meaning one should completely avoid it. "A *śatru* in three places would be death" means that if there is a *śatru* at the beginning, middle, and end of the mantra, then death occurs, or "the failure of the task," meaning the destruction of the purpose, occurs. // 2.19 //
That which is an enemy at the beginning is "siddha" (accomplished) in the middle; that which ends at the conclusion is "sādhya" (to be accomplished).
It should be stated that [the latter] results in very little fruit with great difficulty. (2.20)

Vivaraṇa: “‘Enemy,’ and so forth. When the enemy [syllable] comes first in the calculation of the *āya*, the *siddha* [syllable] occurs in the middle of the mantra. If the *sādhya* [syllable] is at the end of the mantra—that is, if the *sādhya* is at the end of the mantra—then it “occurs with great difficulty”; that is, it arises with great effort—extreme hardship—and yields little fruit. The particle *ca* is used for conjunction. “In this manner” (*iti*) is how it should be explained. (2.20)
If there is an enemy at the beginning, and in the middle there is the attainment of the pair of successes, whatever task was undertaken at the outset—all that indeed perishes in the end. (2.21)
Commentary:

“If there is an enemy at the end” means if there is an adversary (the letter *śa*) at the end of the mantra. “In the first and in the middle, there is the falling of a pair of Siddhas” means if there is the occurrence of a pair of Siddhas at the beginning of the mantra and in its middle. “Whatever task was previously produced”—whatever task of such a kind was previously produced in the mantra, having immeasurable fruit—“all that perishes at the end”; that entire task, having produced its fruit, meets with destruction at the end—that is, at the conclusion. (2.21)

Where one observes that a task is either accomplished, well-accomplished, or obstructed by an enemy, it will result in intense suffering and misfortune; therefore, one should avoid such an undertaking. (2.22)
Vivaraṇa:

“Alternatively” (*athavā*) means in another manner. “Siddha” refers to the word *siddha*; “susiddha” refers to the word *susiddha*. “Separated by an enemy” (*ripuṇāntaritaṃ*) means separated by an enemy-word. If it is “observed therein”—that is, if it is seen within a mantra—then it becomes “powerful in causing suffering and misfortune,” meaning abundant in afflictions and calamities. Having understood this, one should “avoid the mantra,” that is, one should completely abandon the practice of its accomplishment. // 2.22 //
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Sakalīkaraṇa," in the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri, the crest-jewel of poets in both languages. || 2 ||
The third chapter: The Section on the Sequence of the Goddess’s Worship. || 3 ||
One should perform pacification, hatred, subjugation, binding, summoning, and immobilization by means of illumination, sprouts, encapsulation, confinement, stringing together, and interlacing. (3.1)
Vivaraṇa:

By means of *dīpana* (illumination), one should perform pacification (*śāntika*); by means of *pallava* (sprout), one should perform inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*); by means of *sampuṭa* (enclosure), one should perform subjugation (*vaśya*); by means of *rodhana* (obstruction), one should perform binding (*bandha*); by means of *grathanā* (stringing together), one should perform the attraction of women; by means of *vidarbhaṇa* (interlacing), one should perform the paralysis of anger and so forth. // 3.1 //
Now, the explanation of the illuminators (*dīpana*) and so forth:
first, the placement of the name is the illuminator; at the end, the *pallava* is to be known.
That which is situated between those two is the *sampuṭa*; furthermore, that which occurs at the beginning, middle, and end is the *rodha*. (3.2)
Grathana is [the mantra] interspersed with other groups; vidarbha occurs when [the mantra] is situated between two syllables.
Having understood these means for performing the six rites, the practitioner of mantra should perform their application. 3.3.

*Vivaraṇa*: “The insertion of the name at the beginning is the *dīpana*”: the insertion of the name at the beginning of the mantra should be known as the *dīpana*. “And at the end, it is to be known as the *pallava*”: the insertion of the name at the end of the mantra is to be known as the *pallava*. “That which is situated in the middle of that is the *sampuṭa*”: the name inserted in the middle of that mantra is the *sampuṭa*. “Then, occurring at the beginning, middle, and end, it is the *rodha*”: thereafter—at the beginning, middle, and end of the mantra—the insertion of the name is the *rodha*.

‘Grathana is the interlacing of syllables’: one syllable of the mantra and one syllable of the name; such an interlacing of syllables is what is called *grathana*. ‘*Vidarbha* is situated between two syllables’: the placement of the name after each pair of syllables of the mantra is *vidarbha*. ‘This is the performance of the six rites (*ṣatkarmakaraṇa*)’: having understood—that is, having realized—this procedure for the performance of the six rites beginning with pacification (*śānti*), the practitioner of mantras should carry out the practice. (3.2–3)
Having fully understood the distinctions between direction, time, mudrā, posture, and fresh leaves, that mantra-practitioner should perform the recitation;
otherwise, his mantra will not succeed. Let him remain constantly engaged in recitation and fire-offerings.
Vivaraṇa:

Regarding the passage beginning with "direction, time," etc.: direction (*dik*), time (*kāla*), mudrā, seat (*āsana*), and sprout (*pallava*) constitute "direction, time, mudrā, seat, and sprout" (*dikkālamudrāsanapallavāḥ*). Having thoroughly understood—that is, having correctly known—the "distinction" (*bheda*), which is the detailed exposition, of these [five], that "mantrin"—the practitioner of mantras—should recite, meaning he should perform the *japa*.

"And his mantra is not accomplished otherwise. "Otherwise"—that is, in the absence of a thorough understanding of the distinctions of direction, time, and so forth—his mantra, "is not accomplished," meaning it does not attain success (*siddhi*). "Even if he remains constantly performing recitation and fire-offerings": even while remaining constantly engaged in recitation and fire-offerings, he still does not succeed. (3.4)

Facing the directions of Soma, Yama, Amara, Hara, Agni, Marut, and Nirṛti, one should perform subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākarṣaṇa), immobilization (stambhana), prohibition (niṣedha), inciting enmity (vidveṣa), causing movement (calana), pacification (śāntika), and nourishment (puṣṭi).
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), immobilization (*stambhana*), prohibition (*niṣedha*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), causing movement (*calana*), pacification (*śāntika*), and nourishment (*puṣṭi*)—these are the ritual acts (*karmāṇi*). “Facing the directions of Soma, Yama, Amara, Hara, Agni, Marut, Abdhi, and Nirṛti. “Soma”: facing north, the act of subjugation; “Yama”: facing south, the act of attraction; “Amara”: facing east, the act of immobilization; “Hara”: facing the northeast (*īśāna*), the act of prohibition; “Agni”: facing the southeast, the act of inciting enmity.

Facing the direction of the Maruts—that is, facing the northwest—one performs the rite of *calana* (causing movement) or *uccāṭana* (expulsion). Facing the ocean—that is, facing the west—one performs the *śāntika* rite (the rite for pacification). Having one’s face toward the direction of Nirṛti—that is, facing the southwest—one performs the *pauṣṭika* rite (the rite for nourishment). Thus, assuming these respective directions, one should perform the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and the others. 3.5.
In the forenoon, rites of subjugation are performed; at midday, the destruction of affection;
in the afternoon, the rite of eradication; and at twilight, the rite of prohibition.
One should employ the left hand for rites of pacification at midnight, and likewise for rites of enrichment at dawn;
however, one should employ the right hand for all other rites, excluding those of subjugation.
Vivaraṇa:

Regarding the passage beginning with “in the forenoon” (*pūrvāhṇe*): one should perform the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and immobilization (*stambhana*) during the forenoon in the spring season. “At midday, the destruction of affection”: one should perform the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) at midday in the summer season. “Exorcism (*uccāṭana*) in the afternoon”: one should perform exorcism in the afternoon during the rainy season; the word *ca* is used for conjunction. “At twilight, the performer of prohibitions”: one should perform the rite of prohibition (*niṣedha*) at twilight in the autumn season.

‘And the rite of pacification at midnight’: one should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) at midnight during the winter season; the word ‘and’ (*ca*) serves as a conjunction. ‘Likewise, the rite of enrichment at dawn’: at the time of dawn during the cool season (*śiśira*), one should perform the rite of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*). ‘Excluding the rite of subjugation’: setting aside the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*). ‘Other rites’, namely other rites of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), ‘one should perform with the right hand’—that is, with the right hand; the meaning is that one should perform the rite of subjugation specifically with the left hand. (3.6–7)
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the ritual action.

The mudrās of the hook, the lotus, the awakening sprout, the pure conch, and the vajra should be employed at the time of summoning, subjugation, pacification, causing enmity, obstruction, and slaying. (3.8)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Aṅkuśa’ refers to the goad-mudrā for the rite of summoning (ākarṣaṇa); ‘Saroja’ refers to the lotus-mudrā for the rite of subjugation (vaśya); ‘Bodha’ refers to the knowledge-mudrā for the rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika); ‘Pravāla’ refers to the sprout-mudrā for the rite of causing enmity (vidveṣaṇa), [performed] with the syllable *phaṭ*; ‘Sacchaṅkha’ refers to the correct conch-mudrā for the rite of obstruction (stambhana); ‘Vajra’ refers to the thunderbolt-mudrā for the occasion of slaying (vadha), that is, for the occasion of prohibition. Thus, these mudrās “should be” employed in the performance of the six rites.
The staff, the svastika, the lotus, the cock, the vajra, the high seat, and the auspicious throne;
their colors are like the rising sun, the moon, smoke, turmeric, and white. (3.9)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Daṇḍa’ refers to the staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*) for the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); ‘Svastika’ refers to the swastika posture (*svastikāsana*) for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*); ‘Paṅkaja’ refers to the lotus posture (*paṅkajāsana*) for the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); ‘Kukkuṭa’ refers to the cock posture (*kukkuṭāsana*) for the rites of causing hatred (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*); ‘Kuliśa’ refers to the thunderbolt posture (*vajrāsana*) for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*); and ‘Uccabhadrapīṭha’ refers to the broad auspicious throne posture (*vistīrṇabhadrapīṭhāsana*) for the rite of prohibition (*niṣedha*). These postures are to be employed in the performance of the six rites.

‘Udayārka’ is reddish in color for the rite of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); ‘rakta’ is the color of the hibiscus flower for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*); ‘śaśadhara’ is the color of moonstone for the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); ‘dhūma’ is smoky-colored for the rites of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*); ‘haridrā’ is yellow for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*); and ‘asita’ is black for the rite of prohibition (*niṣedha*). These are the colors to be employed when performing the six rites. Thus, the distinctions regarding the colors of the seats have been described. (3.9)
In rites of inciting enmity, attraction, and agitation, one should employ *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* at the end, and *phaṭ*.
In subjugation, one uses *vaṣaṭ*; in the destruction of enemies, *ghe ghe*; and in rites of pacification and nourishment, *svāhā* and *svadhā*.
*Vivaraṇa*:

Regarding “in causing enmity” and so forth: for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), the suffix *huṃ* should be employed. For attracting (*ākarṣaṇa*), the suffix *vauṣaṭ* should be employed at the end. For eradication (*uccāṭana*), the suffix *phaṭ* should be joined. In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), the suffix *vaṣaṭ* should be joined. And for the destruction of enemies (*vairivadha*), the suffix *ghe ghe* should be joined. Because of the word “and” (*ca*), for paralyzing (*stambhana*), the suffix *ghe ghe* should be joined. For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the suffix *svāhā* should be joined. For rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the suffix *svadhā* should be joined.
Thus, these sprouts are to be employed in the performance of the six rites. // 3.10 //
For the purpose of pacification and other rites, the wise one should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times using beads made of crystal, coral, pearl, gold, and putrajīva fruit.
Vivaraṇa:

With beads made of crystal for rites of pacification (*śāntika*); with beads made of coral for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); with beads made of pearls for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); with beads made of gold (*cāmīkara*) for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*); and with beads made of *putrajīvaka* for the rites of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). With these beads, the wise one (*budhaḥ*) should perform “one hundred and eight recitations” (*aṣṭottaraśatajāpyam*)—that is, one hundred and eight recitations—for the purpose of pacification and so forth. // 3.11 //
One should employ [the fingers] in sequence for liberation, sorcery, pacification, subjugation, and attraction;
the joints of the fingers, beginning with the thumb, are moved by the thumb. (3.12)

Vivaraṇa: Regarding the phrase “the fingers beginning with the thumb”: starting with the thumb, one should employ the fingers in rites such as liberation (*mokṣa*). How? “Successively,” that is, in the proper sequence. “The jewels” refers to the jewels previously mentioned; they are “moved by the thumb. One seeking liberation should move them with the thumb. In the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*), one should move them with the index finger; in rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), with the middle finger; in the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), with the ring finger; and in the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should move them with the little finger. // 3.12 //
Thus, according to the text, the six types of action have been explained through the distinctions of direction, time, and so forth.
Now the extraction of the yantra for the house of worship of the Goddess is prescribed:
one should draw this yantra with fragrant substances using a golden stylus; it is square, extensive, provided with three lines, and has four doors. (3.13)

Vivaraṇa: ‘Caturasraṃ’ means perfectly square. ‘Vistīrṇaṃ’ means extensive. ‘Rekhātrayasaṃyutaṃ’ means joined with three lines. ‘Caturdvāraṃ’ means endowed with four gates. ‘Vilikhet’ means one should draw it specifically. ‘Surabhidravyaiḥ’ means with fragrant substances such as saffron, musk, and so forth. ‘Yantram idaṃ’ refers to this yantra of the Goddess. ‘Hemalekhanyā’ means with a golden stylus. // 3.13 //
Homage to Dharaṇendra; homage to the one who covers below, and likewise homage to the one who covers above;
homage to the one who covers the lotus—the mantras beginning with the Vedas and Māyā.
Vivaraṇa:

"Homage to Dharaṇendra"—this is the mantra for the eastern gate. "Homage to Adhacchadana"—this is the mantra for the southern gate. "In that manner" (tathā) means by that same method. "Homage to Ūrdhvacchadana"—this is the mantra for the western gate. "Homage to Padmacchadana"—this is the mantra for the northern gate. "These mantras" (etān mantrān): in what manner are they? "Beginning with the Veda and beginning with Māyā," meaning those beginning with the syllable Oṃ and those beginning with the syllable Hrīṃ. (3.14)
Having drawn these in sequence for the purpose of protecting the seats at the eastern and other gates,
one should draw the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, at the end of the first line.
Vivaraṇa:

In this verse, the first half is to be connected with what precedes it, and the second half is to be connected with what follows. Having "inscribed" (pravilikhya)—that is, having written down clearly—"these" (etān) mantras of the gatekeepers beginning with Dharaṇendra mentioned previously, "in sequence" (kramaśaḥ), namely in the order of east, south, west, and north. For what purpose? "For the sake of protecting the pedestals at the eastern and other gates" (pūrvādidvārapīṭharakṣārtham).

One should write: *oṃ hrīṃ dharaṇendrāya namaḥ* in the eastern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ adhacchadanāya namaḥ* in the southern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ ūrdhvacchadanāya namaḥ* in the western direction; and *oṃ hrīṃ padmacchadanāya namaḥ* in the northern direction—thus on the pedestals of the four doors. Now, for the explanation of the latter half: “one should draw the ten guardians of the directions” means one should properly draw the ten world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Which ones? “Indra and the others,” beginning with Indra.
‘At the end of the first line’: at the end of the first line among the three previously mentioned lines. // 3.15 //
One should place the letters *la-ra-śa-ṣa-va-ya-sa-ha* together with the bindu, accompanied by the lords of the eight directions,
preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, in the upper and lower coverings known as *oṃ-hrīṃ*.
Vivaraṇa:

"The letters *la*, *ra*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *va*, *ya*, *sa*, and *ha* (*laraśaṣavayasaha*)"; these are the letters, thus "the letters *laraśaṣavayasaha*" (*laraśaṣavayasahavarṇān*). "Accompanied by the *bindu*" (*sabindukān*): those which exist together with the *bindu* are "with *bindu*" (*sabindukāḥ*), [meaning] them. Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Joined with the eight lords of the directions" (*aṣṭadikpatisametān*): conjoined with the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*).

"Ending with the praṇava and namas," refers not only to the world-protectors, but also to those known as "Oṃ Hrīṃ Adhacchadana" and "Ūrdhvacchadana," namely: "Oṃ Hrīṃ Adhacchadanāya Namaḥ" and "Oṃ Hrīṃ Ūrdhvacchadanāya Namaḥ."

The sequence for the installation of the World Guardians (Lokapālas): *Oṃ laṃ indrāya namaḥ*—thus in the east. *Oṃ raṃ agnaye namaḥ*—thus in the southeast. *Oṃ śaṃ yamāya namaḥ*—thus in the southern direction. *Oṃ ṣaṃ nairṛtyāya namaḥ*—thus in the southwest direction. *Oṃ vaṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*—thus in the western direction. *Oṃ yaṃ vāyave namaḥ*—thus in the northwest direction. *Oṃ saṃ kuberāya namaḥ*—thus in the northern direction.

"Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Īśāna"—thus in the northeastern direction; "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the lower covering"—thus below; "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the upper covering"—thus above; one should write [these mantras]. Such is the sequence for the installation of the ten guardians of the directions. // 3.16 //
One should draw the deities beginning with Jaya and beginning with Jambha in the cardinal and intermediate directions respectively;
they are preceded by the Praṇava and the three forms [of the deity], ending with "namaḥ" at the end of the central line.

*Vivaraṇa*: "In the cardinal and intermediate directions" means in the primary and secondary quarters. "Successively" means according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions. "The deities Jayā and others, Jambhā and others" refers to the deities beginning with Jayā in the four cardinal directions and the deities beginning with Jambhā in the four intermediate directions. Of what nature are they? "Preceded by the *praṇava* and the three forms," meaning preceded by *oṃ* and *hrīṃ*. Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Ending with *namaḥ*," meaning having the word *namaḥ* at their conclusion. Where? "At the end of the middle line," one should write them at the end of the middle line previously drawn in the east. // 3.17 //
The goddesses are Ādyā, Jayā, Vijayā, and likewise Aparājitā;
these deities are Jambhā, Mohā, Stambhā, and Stambhinī. (3.18)
Commentary:

‘Ādyā’ means the first; ‘Jayā’ is the one named Jayā; ‘Vijayā’ is the one named Vijayā; ‘Tathā’ (in that manner) refers to the one named Ajitā; ‘Ca’ (and) is used as a conjunction; ‘Aparājitā Devyaḥ’ refers to the goddesses of the directions known as Aparājitā. ‘Jambhā’ is the one named Jambhā; ‘Mohā’ is the one named Mohā; ‘Stambhā’ is the one named Stambhā; and ‘Stambhinī’ is the one named Stambhinī—these are the deities of the intermediate directions. These are the eight goddesses.

One should write: *oṃ hrīṃ jaye namaḥ* in the eastern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ vijaye namaḥ* in the southern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ ajite namaḥ* in the western direction; *oṃ hrīṃ aparājite namaḥ* in the northern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ jambhe namaḥ* in the south-eastern direction; *oṃ hrīṃ mohe namaḥ* in the south-western direction; *oṃ hrīṃ stambhe namaḥ* in the north-western direction; and *oṃ hrīṃ stambhini namaḥ* in the north-eastern direction. This is the sequence for establishing the lines for the eight goddesses in the center. 3.18.
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus, [bearing] the name Anaṅgakamalā, as well as Padmagandhā, who has a lotus-like face and wears a garland of lotuses. (3.19)
Vivaraṇa:

"In the midst of that" means in the center of the mandala consisting of the three lines previously drawn; "an eight-petaled lotus" means an eight-petaled kamala; "named Anaṅgakamalā" means one whose name is Anaṅgakamalā, [to be written] upon its petals; and "one should write" means one should write specifically; "Padmagandhā" means one named Padmagandhā; "Padmāsyā" means one named Padmāsyā; and "Padmamālikā" refers to the one called Padmamālā. // 3.19 //
Next, one should draw Madanonmādinī, then the one known as Kāmoddīpanā, then the one called Padmavarṇā, and thereafter Trailokyakṣobhiṇī.
Vivaraṇa:

One should properly write ‘Madanonmādinī’—that is, the one named Madanonmādinī; ‘afterwards,’ immediately following that, one should write ‘Kāmoddīpanasaṃjñikā’—that is, the one named Kāmoddīpanā; then one should write ‘Padmavarṇākhyā’—that is, the one designated by the name Padmavarṇā; and after that, one should write ‘Trailokyakṣobhiṇī. // 3.20 //
Preceded by the syllable *tejo hrīṃ* and ending with the word *namaḥ*,
one should assign [the letters] from *a* to *ha* to the filaments.
Vivaraṇa:

The first half of this verse is to be connected with what precedes it, while the second half is to be connected with what follows. “*Tejohrīṃkāra*” means *oṃkāra* and *hrīṃkāra*. “*Pūrvoktāḥ*” refers to those eight goddesses of the directions mentioned previously; they are thus “preceded by *oṃ* and *hrīṃ*. What are their characteristics? They are “ending with the word *namaḥ*,” meaning they conclude with the word *namaḥ*.

The extraction of these [mantras] is as follows: *oṃ hrīṃ anaṅgakamalāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ padmagandhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ padmāsyāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ padmamālāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ madanonmādinyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ kāmoddīpanāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ padmavarṇāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ trailokyakṣobhiṇyai namaḥ*. These are to be established in the eight petals starting from the east.

Now the latter half [of the verse] is explained: "From the letter *a* to the letter *ha*" means starting with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *ha*; "in the filaments" means in the center of the pericarp; "one should employ" means one should arrange them accordingly. // 3.21 //
Now follows the sequence for the installation of the four wheels of the Goddess:
Bhuvaneśa conjoined with devotion, and then the peak-syllable (kūṭa) of the Goddess conjoined with the four digits (kalās).
The four groups of syllables ending with *namaḥ* should be placed outside the lotus in the directions starting from the east.

Commentary: ‘Endowed with devotion’ means accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*. What is it? ‘The Lord of the World,’ which is the syllable *hrīṃ*. ‘Endowed with four parts’ means accompanied by the four parts *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, and *ai*. What is that? ‘The peak-syllable,’ which is the letter *kṣa*. ‘Then,’ immediately thereafter, ‘the four letters of the Goddess,’ the four syllables of Padmāvatī, ‘ending with *namaḥ*’—that is, ending with the word *namaḥ*—‘are to be placed. Where? ‘In the directions beginning with the East,’ in the four cardinal directions starting from the east. Where [on the diagram]? ‘Outside the lotus,’ in the area outside the eight-petaled lotus.

The extraction of the mantras: one should write "Oṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ pa namaḥ" in the eastern direction, "Oṃ hrīṃ kṣīṃ dmā namaḥ" in the southern, "Oṃ hrīṃ kṣūṃ va namaḥ" in the western, and "Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaiṃ tī namaḥ" in the northern direction. // 3.22 //
"Let this be the fourfold wheel of Queen Padmāvatī; let her perform its worship daily with the fivefold offerings. (3.23)
Vivaraṇa:

"This" has been stated: "There should be a fourfold wheel for Queen Padmāvatī," meaning there should be a fourfold wheel belonging to Queen Padmāvatī. "With the five offerings," that is, by means of the five distinctions beginning with invocation; "worship" means adoration; "constantly" means at all times; "of her," that is, of Queen Padmāvatī; "thus," in this manner, "he should perform" the worship. // 3.23 //
The wise declare that the fivefold service consists of the invocation of the Goddess, her installation, her bringing into proximity, her worship, and her dismissal. (3.24)

Vivaraṇa: ‘Invocation’ is the invocation of the Goddess; ‘Installation’ is the installation of the Goddess; ‘Bringing into Presence’ is the bringing of the Goddess into presence; ‘likewise’ means in that manner; ‘Worship’ is the veneration of the Goddess; ‘Dismissal’ is the dismissal of the Goddess; ‘the wise’ are the learned ones; ‘this fivefold service’ refers to this set of five offerings; ‘they say’ means they declare. // 3.24 //
"Oṃ hrīṃ, homage be to you, O Blessed Lady Padmāvatī! Come, come! Saṃ vauṣaṭ!
With this mantra, one should perform the invocation while recollecting the Goddess. (3.25)
Vivaraṇa:
“Oṃ hrīṃ namo ’stu bhagavati padmāvati ehi ehi saṃ vauṣaṭ”—with this mantra, recollecting—that is, contemplating—the goddess Padmāvatī, one should perform the invocation of the goddess. // 3.25 //
One should join the two *tiṣṭhat*s and the two ending in *ṭha* for the act of making [the deity] stay;
one should join the word *bhava* with *saṃnihitā* and *mama vaṣaṭ* for the act of bringing [the deity] near. (3.26)
*Vivaraṇa*:

One should “join together” (*saṃyojayeta*), that is, properly apply, the “two [words] ending in *sthā*” (*tiṣṭhadvitayaṃ*), namely the two words *tiṣṭha tiṣṭha* mentioned previously, and the “two [letters] ending in *ṭha*” (*ṭhāntadvayam*), namely the two *ṭha*-letters as *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. Where? “In the act of making stay” (*sthitīkaraṇe*), that is, in the installation of the Goddess. [One should join] the word “be present for me” (*saṃnihitā bhava*) and “*vaṣaṭ*” (*vaṣaḍ iti*) at the beginning of the previously mentioned mantra—that is, the phrase *mama saṃnihitā bhava bhava vaṣaṭ* should be added. Where? “In the act of bringing near” (*saṃnidhīkaraṇe*), that is, in the preparation for the worship of the Goddess.
"Take, take the perfumes and so forth—homage! O you who perform the ritual of worship! "Go, go to your own place"—this should be recited three times during the dismissal. (3.27)
Vivaraṇa:

“‘Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gandhādīn, namaḥ’—this should be added before the previously mentioned mantra. Where? ‘In the ritual procedure for worship,’ that is, in the rite of adoring the Goddess. ‘Svasthānaṃ gaccha gaccha, jaḥ’—this should be added three times before the previously mentioned mantra; one should append ‘svasthānaṃ gaccha gaccha jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ’ three times. Where? ‘In her dismissal,’ that is, in the dismissal of the Goddess. (3.27)
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ namo 'stu bhagavati padmāvati ehi ehi saṃ vauṣaṭ. This is the invocation.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage be to you, O Blessed One Padmāvatī! Stay, stay! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! Thus is the rite of stabilization.
Oṃ hrīṃ! Homage be to you, O Blessed One Padmāvatī! Be present, be present for me, vaṣaṭ! Thus is the invocation of presence.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage be to you, O Blessed One Padmāvatī! Accept, accept the perfumes and other offerings; homage! Thus is the ritual for worship.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage be to you, O Blessed One Padmāvatī! Go, go to your own place! Jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ! Thus is the dismissal.
Such is the sequence of the five offerings.
Through the practice of inhalation (pūraka) and exhalation (recaka), the wise one should perform the rites of invocation and dismissal;
through retention (kumbhaka), he should perform the acts of making [the deity] face the worship and of stabilization.
Vivaraṇa:

"Through the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*), the wise one should perform the invocation and dismissal. Through the practice of inhalation, the "wise one"—that is, the learned practitioner—should perform the invocation of the Goddess. Through the practice of exhalation, he should perform the dismissal of the Goddess. "The acts of making [the deity] face the worship and of establishing [her] are performed through retention (*kumbhaka*). One should perform the acts of bringing the Goddess into proximity for worship and of establishing her presence by means of the practice of retention. (3.28)
"Brahmā and the other lords of the world, the syllable *hraiṃ*, the sky [the letter *ha*], ending with *ṣa* and joined with *mada* [the letter *na*];
and upon the lotus, the lotus-waist—this is the root mantra ending in *namaḥ*. (3.29)
Vivaraṇa:

“Brahmādi” means *oṃ* and so forth; “lokanātham” means the syllable *hrīṃ*; “hraimkāram” means the seed-syllable *hraim*; “vyoma” means the letter *ha*. Of what nature is it? “Ṣāntamadanopetaḥ”: the end of *ṣa* (the letter *sa*) and *madana* (the syllable *klīṃ*); joined with these two, it is “ṣāntamadanopetaḥ. How so? It is *hsklīṃ*. “Padme” is a word; *ca* is for conjunction; “padmakaṭini” is the word *padmakaṭinī*; “namontagaḥ” means that at the end is the word *namaḥ*.
‘This is the root mantra’: this mantra is to be known as the root mantra of the goddess Padmāvatī. // 3.29 //
The extraction of the mantra: oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hsklīṃ padme padmakaṭini namaḥ.
The goddess Padmā is accomplished by reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times with lotus flowers;
or else, by reciting it over red oleander flowers together with their stalks.

Vivaraṇa: “She is accomplished” (*sidhyati*) means she becomes perfected. Who? “The goddess Padmā” (*padmādevī*), that is, the goddess Padmāvatī. By what means? “By the recitation of three hundred thousand” (*trilakṣajāpyena*), that is, by the recitation of three hundred thousand [times]. Of what? “Of lotus flowers” (*padmapuṣpāṇām*), that is, of thousand-petaled flowers. Alternatively, in their absence, she becomes perfected “by the recitation of the flowers of the red karavīra together with their stalks” (*aruṇakaravīrakasavṛntapuṣpaprajāpyena*), that is, by the recitation of blossoms of the red karavīra accompanied by their stalks. // 3.30 //
"Brahmā, Māyā, the syllable *hraiṃ*, the sky (*vyoma*) with the syllable *klīṃ* above it,
and *śrīṃ*— they say that the mantra 'Obeisance to Padmā' is the six-syllabled Vidyā. (3.31)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Brahma’ is the syllable *oṃ*; ‘māyā’ is the syllable *hrīṃ*; ‘ca’ (and) is used in the sense of conjunction; ‘hraim’ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); ‘vyoma’ is the letter *ha*. Of what nature is this *vyoma*? It is “situated above the syllable *klīṃ*,” meaning it stands upon the syllable *klīṃ*; thus [the sequence is] *hsklīm*. ‘Śrīṃ’ is the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*; ‘padme’ is the word *padme*; ‘namaḥ’ is the word *namaḥ*. They say that this aforementioned mantra is the six-syllabled vidyā; they declare it to be the six-syllabled knowledge (*vidyā*).
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hsklīṃ śrīṃ padme namaḥ. This is the six-syllable mantra. 3.31.
The wise call this three-syllabled mantra "Vāgbhava," "Cittanātha," and the syllable "Hauṃ" with the letter *ṣa* at its head, joined by two *bindus*. (3.32)

‘Vāgbhava’ is the syllable *aiṃ*; ‘Cittanātha’ is the syllable *klīṃ*; ‘ca’ is used as a conjunction; ‘Hauṃkāra’ is the syllable *haum*. Of what nature is it? ‘Ṣāntamūrdhagam’: the end of the letter *ṣa* is the letter *sa*, and that which goes to its head (*mūrdhagam*) is situated above the *sa*. ‘Bindudvayayutam’: joined with two dots, i.e., conjoined with the *visarga*. Thus, the seed-syllable is *hsauḥ*. ‘This three-syllabled one’: this *vidyā* consisting of three syllables. ‘The wise ones’ (*vibudhāḥ*): the learned. ‘They say’ (*prāhuḥ*): they declare pre-eminently. // 3.32 //
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ hsauḥ namaḥ. This is the three-syllable mantra.
The letter at the end of the class [na], which is the Jina on the side, and that which is situated below it is Dharaṇendra;
the fourth vowel with a bindu shall be known as Padmāvatī. (3.33)
Vivaraṇa:

The letter at the end is *ha*; that *ha* is known as Pārśvajina. The *ra* situated on the palm (the base) is known as Dharaṇendra. The fourth vowel is *ī*; when accompanied by the bindu (*anusvāra*), it becomes known as Padmāvatī. Thus, *hrīṃ* is the single-syllable vidyā-mantra. // 3.33 //
This vidyā, which deludes the people of the three worlds, begins with the syllable *praṇava* and ends with *namaḥ*.
Known by the name "Ekākṣarī," it constantly bestows fruit upon the one who recites it.
Commentary:

This "Vidyā" (knowledge-mantra) which has been described is that which "deludes the people of the three worlds," meaning it causes delusion among the beings of the triple universe. Of what nature is it? It is "preceded by the Praṇava and ending with the word Namaḥ," meaning it begins with the syllable *Oṃ* and concludes with the word *Namaḥ*. What is its name? Its designation is "Ekākṣarī" (the Single-Syllabled). It is "always bestowing fruit upon the one who recites it," meaning it grants results for one who performs its recitation at all times. // 3.34 //
The mantra is: Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ; this is the single-syllable [mantra].
Now the sequence of the fire-oblation (homa) is described:
having written the name surrounded by the principles (tattvas) on a leaf, one should bury it in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having encircled it externally with the five arrows of Smara, it should further be enclosed by the guardians of the worlds (lokapatis).
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Enveloped by reality” (*tattvāvṛtam*) means surrounded by the syllable *hrīṃ*. What is that? “The name,” namely the name Devadatta. “Having written” (*vilikhya*) means having inscribed it. Where? “On a leaf,” that is, on a copper plate. Having done what? “With the arrows of Smara,” that is, with the arrows of Kāma. Of how many in number? “With five,” namely with these: *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, *saḥ*. “Having completely encircled” (*ābhiveṣṭya*) means having wrapped it all around. “Again” (*punah*) means once more. “On the outside” (*bāhye*) means outside of the name. “To be entered by the Lord of the World” (*lokapatipraveṣṭyam*) means having made it surrounded by the syllable *hrīṃ*.

‘In that homa-pit’: that copper-leaf yantra [should be placed] in the middle of the homa-pit. In what kind of pit? ‘In a triangle’: in a three-cornered one. ‘One should bury’: one should fill it [with the yantra].
By performing thirty thousand oblations of guggulu resin mixed with the three sweets (madhuratrika) and formed into pills the size of chickpeas, the goddess Padmāvatī is accomplished. 3.36.
Vivaraṇa:

“Mixed with the three sweets” means combined with ghee, milk, and sugar; “made of guggulu” means made from yakṣa-incense; “of pills the size of chickpeas. “From thirty thousand oblations” means by the offering of thirty thousand such pills. “Is perfected” means she becomes accomplished. Who? “The goddess Padmāvatī,” the goddess whose crest is a serpent.
In the ritual for propitiating the deity, one should place the word "namaḥ" at the end of the mantra;
but at the time of the fire-oblation (homa), one should employ the word "svāhā" at its end.
Vivaraṇa:

At the end of the mantra—that is, at the conclusion of the mantra—one should join the word "namas," meaning the phrase "namas. Where? In the ritual procedure for propitiating the deity—that is, in the method of propitiating the Goddess’s mantra. Furthermore, at its end—that is, at the conclusion of the mantra-propitiation—and at the time of the fire-oblation (homa), one should employ the word "svāhā," meaning the sound "svāhā. One should join it [to the mantra].
Through one million recitations and burnt offerings, that yakṣa Pārśvayakṣa will certainly become manifest—
he who dwells at the foot of a banyan tree, dark-limbed and three-eyed.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“From ten hundred thousand recitations and burnt offerings” means from ten hundred thousand recitations and *homa* oblations. “He becomes manifest” means he becomes directly perceptible. Who? “That yakṣa named Pārśva. Of what nature is he? “Dwelling at the root of a *nyagrodha* tree,” that is, dwelling at the root of a banyan tree. What is his specific characteristic? “Dark-limbed. Again, of what nature is he? “Three-eyed,” meaning having three eyes. “Certainly” (*nūnam*) means with certainty.
The mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ pārśvayakṣa divyarūpa maharṣaṇa ehi ehi oṃ kroṃ hrīṃ namaḥ. This is the mantra for the ritual procedure of propitiating the Yakṣa.
With his own troops raised up through illusion, that Yakṣa turns back the enemy host standing before him in battle in a mere twinkling of an eye. (3.39)
Commentary:

"By his own armies" means by his own troops. Of what nature are they? "Raised up by means of illusion" (māyāmayasamucchritaiḥ), meaning properly elevated by the construction of a rampart made of the syllable *hrīṃ*. "The host of enemies" refers to the entire multitude of the enemy's forces. Of what nature is it? "Standing in front," meaning positioned ahead of his own army. "He turns away" means he causes them to turn their backs. Who is he? "The Yakṣa," namely the Yakṣa at the side. Where? "In battle," on the ground of the battlefield. How? "In the mere twinkling of an eye," that is, in a single moment.
One should draw the syllable *sānta* (sa), with a *bindu* above and a *repha* (ra) outside; then an elongated eight-petaled lotus.
In the directions, one should write: *aiṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *smareśaḥ*, *gajavaśakaraṇaṃ*, *hrauṃ*, likewise *blaiṃ*, and again *yūṃ*.

Outside, one who worships that which has the four seed-syllables written in the directions—*hrīṃ*, *oṃ*, *namo*, and *arhaṃ*—along with the fire-oblation (*homa*), shall become the beloved of the glory of liberation, and even the entire world will come under his control. (3.40)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Sāntaṃ’ means the letter *ha*, which is the end of the letter *sa*. Of what nature is it? ‘Bindūrdhvarephaṃ’, meaning it is endowed with an *anusvāra* above a *repha* (the letter *ra*). Thus, one should write the seed-syllable *rhaṃ*. ‘Bahir api’ means on the outer region beyond the syllable *rhaṃ*. ‘Vilikhet’ means one should write it specifically. What is it? ‘Āyatāṣṭābjapatram’, meaning the petals of a broad eight-petalled lotus. ‘Dikṣu’ means in the four directions, starting with the east, among those petals.

One should write as follows: ‘Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Smareśaḥ’—‘Aiṃ’ on the eastern petal, ‘Śrīṃ’ on the southern petal, ‘Hrīṃ’ on the western petal, and ‘Klīṃ’ on the northern petal. Then, for the subjugation of elephants, one should write ‘Hrauṃ’, and likewise ‘Blaṃ’ and ‘Yūṃ’ on the four petals in the intermediate directions: ‘Krauṃ’ on the southeast petal, ‘Hrauṃ’ on the southwest petal, ‘Blaṃ’ on the northwest petal in that same manner, and finally ‘Yūṃ’ on the northeast petal. One should write thus.

"Outside" means one should encircle the exterior of that yantra with the syllable *hrīṃ*. "The four seed-syllables written in the directions" refers to the phrase *oṃ namo 'rhaṃ* written in the four cardinal directions starting from the east, along with the four seed-syllables *aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*. "Accompanied by *homa*" means joined with the word *svāhā*. Thus, the mantra is: *oṃ namo 'rhaṃ aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā*.

"He who worships this non-material yantra of the Cintāmaṇi becomes beloved by the lady of liberation (Muktyaṅganā), and even the world itself comes under his control. "Even the world" means the entire universe; "comes under his control" means it becomes submissive to him.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Propitiation of the Goddess," in the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa* composed by the eminent poet in both languages, the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri.
The fourth chapter: The Extraction of the Twelve-Coloring Mantra. || 4 ||
One should draw a twelve-petaled lotus joined with the syllables *mala varayūṃ* as its peak;
in its center, one should write the name accompanied by the syllable *klīṃ*.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“A twelve-petalled lotus” means a lotus endowed with twelve petals. Of what nature is it? “Joined with the syllables *ma*, *la*, *va*, *ra*, and *yūṃ*”: *ma*, *la*, *va*, *ra*, and *yūṃ* are the syllables *malavarayūṃ*; it is joined with these. What [is joined]? “The peak-syllable” (*kūṭa*), which is the letter *kṣa*. Thus, it is *kṣmlvryūṃ*. “In its center, joined with the name”: in the center of *kṣmlvryūṃ*, one should write the name of Devadatta (or whatever the name may be). “One should write” means one should write specifically. Of what nature is it? “Constrained by the syllable *klīṃ*”: one should write it constrained by the syllable *klīṃ* on both sides of that cluster.
One should write the goddesses Jayā and the others in the cardinal directions, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*;
likewise, Jambhā and the others, accompanied by the seed-syllables *jha*, *bha*, *ma*, and *ha*, should be written in the intermediate directions.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“One should draw Jayā and the other goddesses” means one should draw the four deities beginning with Jayā. Where? “In the directions,” that is, in the four cardinal directions. “Preceded by *oṃ* and ending in *svāhā*”: one should write *oṃ jaye svāhā* on the eastern petal, *oṃ vijaye svāhā* on the southern petal, *oṃ ajite svāhā* on the western petal, and *oṃ aparājite svāhā* on the northern petal.

‘Endowed with the clusters of jha, bha, ma, and ha’: *jha*, *bha*, *ma*, and *ha* are *jhabhamahaḥ*; those which are also clusters are *jhabhamahapiṇḍāḥ*, and they are endowed with these, thus *jhabhamahapiṇḍopetāḥ*. Where? ‘In the intermediate directions,’ that is, in the *vidiśas*. Which ones? ‘Jambhā and the others,’ the four goddesses beginning with Jambhā. ‘In the same manner,’ as before, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*.

One should write: "Oṃ jhmlvryūṃ jambhe svāhā" in the southeastern direction; "Oṃ bhmlvryūṃ mohe svāhā" on the petal of the southwest; "Oṃ mmlvryūṃ stambhe svāhā" on the petal of the northwest; and "Oṃ hmlvryūṃ stambhini svāhā" on the petal of the northeast.
Then, one should draw the seed-syllable of Makaradhvaja within the four [petals] from which the leaves have been removed;
it should be restrained by the "subduing of the elephant" mantra and encircled three times with Māyā.
Vivaraṇa:

Regarding the phrase “then, upon the removed petals” (*uddharitadaleṣu tataḥ*): this means after the drawing of the eight petals, [one should act] upon those removed petals. How many in number? “In four,” meaning in those numbering four. “One should write the seed-syllable of Makaradhvaja”: one should write the seed-syllable *klīṃ*. “Restrained by the subduer of elephants” (*gajavaśakaraṇaniruddhaṃ*): restrained by the syllable *krauṃ*. “It should be encircled three times with Māyā”: it should be encircled threefold outside the petals with the syllable *hrīṃ*. “One should do so” (*kuryāt*): let him perform it.
Having inscribed [the mantra] on birch bark with fragrant substances and wrapped it with a red thread, one should place it in a beautiful vessel filled with honey; this bewilders a woman. 4.4.
Vivaraṇa:

“On birch” means on a leaf of the *bhūrja* tree. “With fragrant substances” means with fragrant materials such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and the like. “Having written” means having inscribed this mantra. “Having wrapped with a red thread” means having encircled it with a red thread. “Having placed” means having set it down. Where? “In an unbaked vessel. Of what nature? “Filled with honey,” that is, filled with *mākṣika* honey. “He deludes the woman” means he deludes the female, the wife.
The extraction of its root mantra is as follows:

[p.20] Oṃ kṣmlvryūṃ klīṃ jaye vijaye ajite aparājite jhmlvryūṃ jambhe bhmlvryūṃ mohe mmlvryūṃ stambhe hmlvryūṃ stambhini klīṃ hrīṃ krauṃ vaṣaṭ. For the rite of delusion, there is the *klīṃ-rañjikā* yantra.
One should draw the yantra upon a woman’s skull, placing the Lord of the World (the syllable *hūṃ*) in the position of *klīṃ*;
by heating it at the three junctions of the day with a fire of *khadira* wood, the attraction of women (*rāmā*) will occur.

Vivaraṇa: ‘In the skull of a woman’ means in the skull of a female. ‘One should draw the yantra’ means one should write the yantra previously described. ‘In the place of *klīṃ*’ means in the location where the syllable *klīṃ* was; what [should be written]? One should write the syllable *hrīṃ*, the ‘Lord of the World’. ‘At the three junctions’ means at the three times of day. ‘One should heat it’ means one should perform the heating rite. ‘There will be the attraction of the woman’ means the summoning of the female will occur. By what? ‘By the fire of *khadira* wood,’ that is, by the fire of *khadira* timber. This is the *hrīṃ-rañjikā* yantra for the attraction of women.
One should draw the syllable *huṃ* upon human skin in the place of the *māyā*;
by heating it with poison and blood, one brings about the cessation [of the enemy] within seven days.

*Vivaraṇa*: “In the place of *māyā*”: in the place of the syllable *hrīṃ*. “And” (*ca*) is for conjunction. What? “The *huṃ*-syllable,” that is, the seed-syllable *huṃ*. “One should write” (*vilikhet*): one should inscribe. Where? “On human skin,” one should write on human hide. With what? “With poison and blood,” that is, with the blood of a poisonous donkey. “One should heat it”: one should heat it as previously described. “Within a fortnight” (*pakṣāhāt*): in the middle of a fortnight. “It becomes a performer of prohibition”: it acts as a means of restraint. This is the *huṃ-rañjikā* yantra for the rite of prohibition.
Having written "huṃ" in its proper place, followed by the name ending in "mān" and joined with the letter "ra," this is the yantra for both mortals on a fruit of the *bibhītaka* tree.
Vivaraṇa:

"In the place of *huṃ*" means in the location of the syllable *huṃ* written over the previously prohibited rite. "Ending with *m*" refers to the letter *ya*. "Having written" means having caused it to be inscribed. Of what nature is it? "With *repha*" means accompanied by an upward-pointing *repha* (the letter *r*). "Joined with the name" means conjoined with the name. Of which two? "Of both mortals," certainly. Where? "On a board of *bibhītaka*" means on a board made of the *kalitaru* tree. This *yantra* is to be drawn.
Having wrapped the hair of a horse and a buffalo around two images with faces turned away from each other, one should place them on the ground; this creates enmity between those two.
Vivaraṇa:

“And with the hair of horses and buffaloes” means with the hair of horses and buffaloes; the word “and” (ca) is used for conjunction. “Having wrapped” means having wrapped all around with hair. “Of those standing face-to-face” means of those standing with faces turned downwards. “One should place” means one should deposit. Where? “On the ground,” that is, on the ground of a cremation ground. “He creates enmity between the two” means he effects hostility between those two mortals. This is the *yaṃrañjikā* yantra for the rite of creating enmity.
In the previously described arrangement of syllables, using a pen made from a crow's wing, one should write the letter 'ma' joined with a visarga,
colored with the charcoal of a corpse and poison, which is as red as blood.
Having written the name of the enemy upon a banner-mechanism joined with the excrement of an owl, and having bound it above trees, there is the eradication of the foe. 4.10.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“In the position of the syllables previously mentioned” means in the place of the syllable *rya*, which is written for the rite of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*). “Ending with *m*” refers to the letter *ya*. Of what nature is it? One should write it “joined with the visarga,” that is, endowed with two dots (*bindu*).
