“On the head” (*śīrṣe*) means on the crown; “on the face” (*āsye*) means on the mouth; “on the heart” (*hṛdaye*) means in the region of the heart; “on the navel” (*nābhau*) means in the region of the navel; “on the foot” (*pāde*) means on the two feet. The word “and” (*caḥ*) is used for conjunction. “The arrows of Anaṅga” refers to the five arrows: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*. “Then they should be joined” means they should be applied in sequence to the five locations beginning with the head. “Enchantment through the direct order” (*sammohanam anulomye*) means enchantment by means of meditation starting from the head and ending at the feet.

"One should perform the rite of driving away (*drāvaṇa*) when [the situation] is contrary. One should perform the driving away by meditating on those same five arrows in sequence, starting from the feet up to the top of the head. *Drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*—these are the five arrows for the installation in the natural order of the limbs (*aṅgānulomasthāpana*).
One should give betel, perfumes, and other such items consecrated with the arrows of Smara;
by washing one's own face as well, one shall become the god of love for women. (7.30)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“He should give” (*dadyāt*) means let him give. What? “Betel, fragrance, and so forth” (*tāmbūlagandhādīn*), namely betel, sandalwood, perfumes, flowers, fruits, and the like. Of what nature are they? “Consecrated with the arrows of Smara” (*smarabāṇābhimantritān*), that is, consecrated by the mantra of the arrows of Kāma. Not only are the betel and other items given; “he should also wash his own face” (*kṣālayed ātmavaktraṃ ca*), meaning he should wash his mouth after having consecrated water with that same mantra. “He,” such a person, “would become the Manmatha” (*manmathaḥ bhavet*), the god of love, “for women” (*strīṇām*), for female consorts.
The extraction of the mantra for consecrating those flowers: oṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ hsklīṃ aiṃ nityaklinne madadrave madanāture sarvajanaṃ mama vaśyaṃ kuru kuru vaṣaṭ.
One should simply visualize a single lump of vermilion-colored [mercury] upon the private part of an excellent woman;
by the mere casting of a glance, its melting occurs, and within seven days, there is the attraction of the woman. (7.31)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“One should contemplate” (*vicintayet*) means one should contemplate specifically. What? “Just a single *liṅga-piṇḍa*,” that is, a single syllable *kṣem*. Of what nature? “The color of vermilion,” meaning a color like that of vermilion. Where? “On the private parts of a woman,” that is, in the womb of women. “Its melting” (*tad-drāvaṇaṃ*): that contemplation causes melting. Why? “Merely by the casting of the gaze,” that is, merely by the casting of the gaze of the practitioner of meditation.
It not only causes melting and delusion, but "the attraction of women within seven days" means that it effects the attraction of women within the course of seven days.
Having made a rope from the hair on the head of a Brahmin, he wrapped it around the skull of a hell-being;
then, using the body-unguents, hair, nails, and the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), [he performed the ritual].
Having mixed it with powdered human bone, one should place it in the previously mentioned crucible.
By the recollection of the mantra and by the churning of the bones, it causes fever within seven days. (33) [This constitutes a pair of verses.]
Vivaraṇa:

"With the hair from the head of a Brāhmaṇa" means with the hair from the head of a twice-born man. "Having made a rope" means having fashioned a rope from that hair. "With that" refers to the rope. "A human skull" refers to a hollowed-out human cranium. "Having encircled it" means having wrapped it all around. "The body-powder, hair, nails, and foot-dust of the victim" means having taken the body-powder, hair, nails, and dust from the feet of the person to be targeted. "Mixed with powdered human bone" means combined with the powder of human bones. "Having prepared" means having performed [the mixture].

‘That’ refers to the powder of impurities and so forth. ‘One should cast’ means one should place it. Where? ‘In the previously mentioned crucible,’ that is, in the human skull-cup crucible mentioned earlier. ‘It causes fever’ means it seizes the person to be treated with fever. Why? ‘From the recollection of the mantra,’ that is, from the mental contemplation of the mantra beginning with “Oṃ Caṇḍeśvara. How? ‘Within seven days,’ that is, within the course of seven days. By what means? ‘By Asthimathana,’ which is by churning a stake made of human bone.
The extraction of the mantra is as follows: Oṃ Caṇḍeśvara, with the fierce axe, seize, seize [so-and-so] with fever, Hrīṃ! Kill, kill! Hūṃ Phaṭ Ghe Ghe!
The mantra practitioner should first recite the mantra ten thousand times with *aruṇa* flowers, ending with the fire-oblation for Caṇḍeśvara, while maintaining a humble and disciplined demeanor.
*Vivaraṇa*:

The phrase “to Caṇḍeśvara” (*caṇḍeśvarāya*) refers to the word *caṇḍeśvarāya*. “Ending with the *homa*” means ending with the word *svāhā*. “One should recite” (*saṃjapet*) means one should recite properly. How? With humility and so forth, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*. “Ten thousand” (*sahasradaśakam*) means ten thousand (*daśasahasram*). Who is this? The “mantrin,” that is, the practitioner of mantra. How? “Previously,” during the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*). With what? With “red flowers,” namely, red *karavīra* flowers.
The extraction of the mantra: *Oṃ caṇḍeśvarāya svāhā*. The recitation (*jāpya*) is ten thousand times.
The name [of the deity] is encircled by the letter *ṭa*, the letter *va*, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and half a moon (*ardhaśaśi*).
When cast into hot or cold water, it shall remove fevers caused by heat or cold. (7.35)
Vivaraṇa:

“Ṭāntavakāra” means ṭānta, which is the letter ṭha; vakāra is the syllable va. “Praṇavanam” is the syllable Oṃ. “Jāntaḥ” is the letter jha. “Ardhaśaśipraveṣṭitam” means encircled by a line in the shape of a half-moon. [The name] is “encircled” (praveṣṭitam)—meaning thoroughly surrounded—by these five letters beginning with ṭha. What is that? It is the “name” (nāma) of the person seized by fever.

"It shall remove cold and heat fevers when placed in hot or cold water. This yantra, when placed in the midst of hot water, shall remove cold fever; that same yantra, when placed in the midst of cold water, shall remove heat fever.
Now the procedure for the sacrificial substances is described:
through an oblation of *śāli* rice, unbroken grains, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and sandalwood, there is pacification and nourishment.
By offering karavīra flowers as an oblation, one may bring women under one's control.
Commentary:

"By the oblation of rice, unbroken grains, sprouts of dūrvā grass, and sandalwood" means by the offering of *kalama* rice, unbroken grains, white *dūrvā* sprouts, and fragrant substances (*śrīgandha*). One should perform the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*). "From the oblation of *karavīra* flowers," one should perform the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) for women, that is, for female consorts.
From the daily performance of a fire-offering with mahiṣākṣa and padma, there arises agitation among the city-dwellers;
from the offering of areca-nut fruits and leaves, kings come under one's control.
Commentary:

“From the offering of mahiṣākṣa and padma” means from the burnt offering of guggulu and padma. “Every day there is agitation among the city folk” means that day by day, agitation among the people of the city occurs. “From the offering of kramuka fruit and leaves” means from the offering of areca nut and betel vine leaves. “Kings come under control” means all sovereigns become submissive.
Through oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, there is an increase in grain and wealth;
through oblations of jasmine flowers accompanied by ghee, the people under one's command become submissive.
Vivaraṇa:

"By oblations of sesame and grains" means by offerings of sesame and other such grains. Of what nature are they? "Combined with clarified butter," that is, accompanied by ghee. "There occurs an increase of grain and wealth" means there shall be an increase of grain and wealth. "From the oblation of jasmine blossoms" means from the offering of *mallikā* flowers. Of what nature is it? "With ghee," that is, joined with cow's clarified butter. "The people under one's command become submissive" means the servants and subordinates become obedient.
Through the oblation of a heap of mango fruits mixed with ghee, the sky-walker (khecarī) becomes submissive;
and through the oblation of *brahmapuṣpa* flowers, the *vaṭa*-yakṣiṇī becomes submissive.
Vivaraṇa:

"From the oblation of a heap of mango fruits mixed with clarified butter" means from the offering of a collection of mango fruits combined with *ājya*. "She becomes" means she will be. "The Sky-farer" (*khecarī*) refers to the goddess named Khecarī. "Subdued" means she becomes subject to one's will. "And the Banyan Yakṣiṇī" refers to the goddess named Vaṭayakṣiṇī. "Of Brahma-flowers" means of *palāśa* flowers. "From the oblation" means from the *homa* sacrifice. "She becomes subdued" means she comes under control.
By performing oblations with house-soot, nimba, rāji, salt, and crow’s wing-feathers, even those born from the same womb shall harbor mutual enmity. 7.40.
Vivaraṇa:

‘House-smoke’ means the smoke from a dwelling; ‘nimba’ is the *picumanda* tree; ‘rājī’ is black mustard; ‘lavaṇa’ is sea salt. ‘With these combined’ means joined with these; ‘by offerings made with crow’s wings’ means by offerings made with the feathers of a crow. ‘Of those born from the same womb’ refers to persons produced from a single womb. ‘Api’ (even) signifies certainty. ‘Mutual enmity’—it ‘occurs,’ that is, it arises.
By means of a fire-oblation (homa) using charcoal from a cremation ground mixed with *bībhītaka* fruits, one brings about the death of the enemy host within half a fortnight. (7.41)

Vivaraṇa: [The phrase] "of the cremation ground, the thorny *bībhītaka* tree, charcoal, the house, and smoke" refers to the charnel ground, bones, spirits, trees, charcoal, the dwelling, and smoke. "By means of *homa*" means by means of the fire-oblation. "Occurs" means it arises. What is that? "Death," that is, the state of the five elements. How? "Within a fortnight," that is, from among the days of the lunar half-month. Of whom? "Of the world of enemies," that is, of the host of adversaries.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the section on the mantras for subjugation (*vaśya*), in the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa* composed by the crest-jewel of poets in both languages, the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri. || 7 ||
The eighth [chapter]: The Determination of the Causal Conditions such as the Mirror, etc. || 8 ||
Success is attained through ten thousand recitations, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with the fire-oblation (*homa*);
the mantra for the mirror-sign should be recited starting from the *cala*, *cule*, and *cūle*.
Vivaraṇa:

"It is accomplished" (sidhyati) means it attains success. By what means? "By a thousand recitations. Of what kind? "Multiplied by ten," meaning ten thousand; this is the intended sense. Again, of what kind? "Preceded by the Praṇava and ending with the word Homānta," meaning preceded by the syllable Oṃ and ending with the word Svāhā. The "mantra for the purpose of the mirror" (darpaṇanimittamantraḥ)—that is, the mantra for the purpose of the mirror—is to be recited.

The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ cale cule cūḍe, having entered the limbs of the two maidens, as it truly is, as it is to be conceived, as it is in reality, do not delay; fulfill my hope, fulfill it, svāhā!
One should have two young girls, born of a Brāhmaṇa family and seven years of age, drink cow’s milk over which the mantra has been recited seven times. (8.2)
Vivaraṇa:

"Consecrated seven times" means consecrated seven times with the recited mantra. What [is to be given]? "Cow's milk," that is, the milk of a cow. "One should cause to drink" means one should make them drink. "Of the two girls" means of the two maidens. Of what kind are they? "Born in a Brāhmaṇa family," meaning those produced from a lineage of Brahmins. Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Seven years old," meaning seven years of age. "Of those two" means of both.
Then, having bathed them in the morning and offered flowers and other gifts to them,
he stood upon a ground that had been swept with cow dung so as not to fall upon the earth.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Having bathed” (*saṃsnāpya*) means having properly washed. “Then” (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the bath. “In the morning” (*prātaḥ*) means at the time of dawn. “Having given” (*dattvā*) “to them,” i.e., to the two maidens. “Then” (*atha*) means afterwards. “Flowers and so forth” (*prasūnādīn*) refers to flowers, unbroken rice grains, ointments, and the like. “On the ground” (*bhūmyām*) means on the earth. “Not fallen” (*apatitam*) means not dropped. “Cow dung” (*gomayaṃ*) means dried cow-dung. “On a surface well-swept with that” (*sammārjitabhūtale*) means on a ground thoroughly cleansed by that cow dung. “Staying” (*sthitvā*) means having remained there.
One should place a jar filled with scented water situated within a square mandala;
upon it, one should set a mirror facing westward.
Vivaraṇa:

“Situated in a square maṇḍala” means situated in the center of a perfectly square maṇḍala. Which one? “The flask,” that is, the jar. Of what nature is it? “Filled with scented water,” meaning filled with water mixed with fragrant substances. “Upon it” means upon that full jar. “A mirror” means a looking-glass. “One should place” means one should set it down. How? “Facing west,” that is, directed toward the western direction.
Then, having placed a pair of previously prepared young maidens facing him, he should contemplate the syllable *blūṃ*—enclosed within the *praṇava* (*oṃ*)—in their hearts. (8.5)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Then” (*atha*) means afterwards. “Facing that” (*tadabhimukhe*) means facing that mirror. “The pair of maidens previously envisioned” (*prākkalpitakumārikāyugalam*) refers to the pair of girls who were previously prepared through bathing and other rites. “Having placed them” (*niveśya*) means having established them within that mandala. “Then” (*tataḥ*) means after that. “In their hearts” (*taddhṛdaye*) means in the hearts of that pair of maidens. “The syllable *blūṃ*” (*blūṃkāram*) refers to the seed-syllable *blūm*. “One should contemplate” (*vicintayet*) means one should meditate upon it specifically. How so? “Enclosed by the *praṇava*” (*praṇavasampuṭitam*), meaning contained within the enclosure of the syllable *oṃ*;
that is, *oṃ blūṃ oṃ*, thus enclosed by the *oṃ*-syllable.
Recalling that mantra, which is as gentle as the lunar disc, one should remain oneself;
then, looking at a pair of young girls reflected in a mirror, one should question them. (8.6)
Vivaraṇa:

"Gentle like the lunar disc" means having a gentle form like the orb of the moon. "That mantra" refers to the mantra that is about to be described. "One should remain oneself recollecting it" means the practitioner of the mantra should remain personally [focused] upon it. "A pair of maidens being looked at in a mirror" refers to a pair of young girls. "One should ask" means that which is to be inquired about.
Whatever is seen and whatever is heard, the form and the word therein are just as they appear in a sword, a thumb-nail, water, or a mirror; that is the truth, and it cannot be otherwise. (8.7)
Vivaraṇa:

"That which was seen" means what was seen there; "that which was heard" means what was heard there. "By those two" refers to the two maidens. "There" refers to the cause, such as a sword and so forth. "Form and speech just as [they were]" means in whatever manner the form was seen and the speech was overheard. Where? "In the sword, the thumb, the water, and the mirror"—that is, in the case of the sword and the thumb, in the jar filled with water, and in the case of the mirror. "That is true": everything that was seen and heard is factual.
"It cannot be otherwise": it does not become false in any other way whatsoever.
One should observe signs such as a mirror, a thumb, a lamp, and so forth;
for practitioners of mantra, the mantra is accomplished through eight thousand recitations.
Vivaraṇa:

“One should observe the sign,” meaning one should look at the mirror, the thumb, the lamp, and so forth. “Is accomplished” means one attains success (*siddhi*). “With eight thousand” means with eight thousand [recitations]. Which one? “The mantra,” namely the mantra that is about to be taught. “By recitation” means by the act of chanting. Of whom? “Of the practitioners of mantra,” that is, of those who utter mantras.

The extraction of the mantra for her propitiation: Oṃ namo meru mahāmeru, oṃ namo gaurī mahāgaurī, oṃ namaḥ kālī mahākālī, oṃ indre mahāindre, oṃ jaye mahājaye, oṃ namo vijaye mahāvijaye, oṃ namaḥ paṇṇasamaṇi mahāpaṇṇasamaṇi, descend, descend, O Goddess, descend, descend, svāhā!
Having previously provided a bed of darbha grass and a diet of milk for the two young girls,
he then bathed them in the morning and [offered] white garments, ornaments, and so forth.
Commentary:

“Having given”—what? “A bed of *darbha* grass,” that is, a couch made of *darbha*. “A diet of milk,” meaning a meal consisting of milk. How? “Previously,” at night during the first watch. Of whom? “Of the two maidens. “Then,” immediately after that. “In the morning,” at the time of dawn. “Having bathed them thoroughly,” having caused them to be well-washed. “White garments, ornaments, and so forth,” meaning white clothing, decorations, and the like.
Then one should place this mantra at the locations of the water jar, the mirror, and the young girl;
it consists of the syllables *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ*, which subdue the elephant and bring about discipline, ending with the word *homa*.
Vivaraṇa:
‘In the places of the jar, the mirror, and the maiden’ means in these locations: the placement of the jar, the placement of the mirror, and the placement of the maiden. ‘Then’ means afterwards.

"One should place"—what?—"this mantra," the mantra about to be described: "the subduer of elephants, ending with *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ* and *svāhā*. Here, *oṃ* is designated as "subduer" (*vinaya*), *kroṃ* as "the subduer of elephants" (*gajavaśakaraṇa*), and then *kṣāṃ*, *kṣīṃ*, and *kṣūṃ*; "ending with *homānta*" means ending with the word *svāhā*.
The extraction of the mantra for installation in the three places: Oṃ kroṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ svāhā. One should place this mantra in the three places.
Having consecrated them with the five voids beginning with the *praṇava*, one should give cakes mixed with ghee to those two for them to eat at the place of the maiden’s breasts. (8.11)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“With the five voids beginning with the *praṇava*” means with the five voids, namely *oṃ*, *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hrauṃ*, and *hraḥ*. “Having consecrated” means having recited the mantra. Where? “In the place of the maiden’s breasts,” that is, in the location of the pair of a girl’s breasts. “Of those two” refers to the two maidens. “And” (*ca*) means furthermore. “To eat” means to consume. “One should give” means it should be given. What? “Cakes” (*pūpa*), that is, small pastries. Of what nature? “Mixed with ghee,” meaning combined with clarified butter (*ājya*).
One should observe the form on the thumb of a hand stained with lac-dye, by means of bathing the thumb with oil prepared from the hands. 8.12.
Commentary:

“With the thumb of the hand anointed with lac” means with the right thumb of the mantra-practitioner. “One should gaze at” means one should look upon. What? “The form,” that is, the reflection. By what means? “By oil prepared by the hands,” meaning by oil rubbed between the two hands. Of what nature is it? “By means of washing the thumb,” this refers to the thumb-marked [oil] smeared on the thumb after the mantra has been recited over it.
The Praṇava, the pair of Piṅgalas, and the two Paṇṇattis—this is the Mahāvidyā;
the pair of letters ending in ṭa, along with the homa and the Darpaṇa mantra, have been taught by the Jina. (8.13)

Commentary: ‘Praṇava’ is the syllable *oṃ*. ‘Piṅgalayugalaṃ’ refers to the two words *piṅgala piṅgale*. ‘Paṇṇattidvayaṃ ca’ refers to the two words *paṇṇatti paṇṇatti*. ‘Mahāvidyeyam’ means this is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*). ‘Ṭāntadvayaṃ’ refers to the two *ṭha* letters. ‘Ca’. ‘Homaḥ’ is *svāhā*. Thus is the ‘Darpaṇamantraḥ’, the Mirror Mantra, ‘jinoddiṣṭaḥ’, proclaimed by the Lord of Jinas.
Mantra: Oṃ piṅgala piṅgala paṇṇatti paṇṇatti ṭha ṭha svāhā.

This mantra for the purpose of obtaining a mirror is accomplished through ten thousand recitations with white flowers resembling moonbeams, followed by a fire-offering (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that number. 8.14.

Vivaraṇa: ‘Jāpyam’ means recitation. ‘By thousands of suns’ means by twelve thousand. By what? ‘With white flowers,’ that is, with white blossoms. Of what nature? ‘Resembling moonbeams,’ similar to the rays of the moon. ‘Succeeds’ means it attains accomplishment (siddhi). By what? ‘By an oblation of one-tenth,’ that is, by an oblation consisting of one-tenth of the twelve thousand [recitations]. ‘This is the mantra for the purpose of the mirror’ means this mantra is the means for accomplishing the sign of the mirror.
Having first rubbed a mirror twenty-one times with funeral ashes,
[one should place it] in a new jar filled with fresh water situated upon unbroken grains of śāli rice.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Twenty-one times with the ashes of a funeral pyre” means having crushed—having ground—what? “The mirror. “Situated upon unbroken grains of *śāli* rice” means situated upon an offering of *kalama* rice and unbroken grains. “In a new jar filled with fresh water” means in a new jar filled with water from the river (*agrodaka*).
Having placed that [image] there, he should station a pair of maidens born of a single noble family,
along with one man from among the three [higher] castes who has bathed and is clad in white garments.

Vivaraṇa: ‘Having placed that’ means having established that mirror upon the jar. ‘In that’ means in the vicinity of that jar. ‘A pair of maidens born of one family’ means a pair of daughters produced from a single lineage. Of what quality? ‘Belonging to one of the three castes,’ meaning having obtained a pair of virtuous maidens from among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas; that is one [requirement]. Furthermore, of what nature are they? ‘Bathed,’ meaning having performed their ablutions. ‘Clad in white garments,’ meaning endowed with the wearing of white clothes.
Then, having worshipped the water-pot with perfumes, rice grains, offerings, flowers, and so forth,
and having given betel leaves and other items, he should show a mirror to the two of them.

Vivaraṇa: ‘Having worshipped’ means having worshipped correctly. With what? ‘With perfumes, rice, offerings, flowers, and so forth,’ that is, with the eight kinds of articles for worship, such as perfumes, unbroken grains (akṣata), excellent flowers, lamps, incense, and the like. ‘Then’ means from that [point]. ‘The jar’ refers to the full water-pot (pūrṇakumbha). ‘Having given betel and so forth’ means having given betel, perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, and the like. ‘One should show the mirror. ‘To them’ means to the two young girls (kumārikā).
While reciting the mantra, one should remain standing and likewise ask the pair of young girls;
they will tell what has been seen and heard, as well as the form and the speech, like reflections at the edge of a mirror.
Vivaraṇa:

"Reciting the mantra" means uttering the mantra. "He should stay" means he should dwell [there]. "A pair of young girls" means a pair of maidens. "In that manner" means by that method. "He should ask" means he should pose a question. "He tells what is seen and heard" means he relates everything that has been seen and everything that has been heard. "Form and speech at the edge of the mirror" means he tells whatever form is seen and whatever speech is heard in the mirror. Thus ends the descent of the mirror. Now, the lamp-seated practice (dīpaniṣadyā) is described:
When the mantra is recited with true devotion eight thousand times using jasmine flowers before the Victorious Lord Śrī Vīranātha, the goddess Sundarī is accomplished. 8.19.
*Vivaraṇa*:

"With eight thousand" means with groups of eight thousand. "With *jātī* flowers" means with blossoms of the *mālatī*. "In front of the Lord Jina Śrī Vīranātha" means before the Jina Lord Śrī Vardhamāna. "When recited" means when the recitation (*jāpya*) has been performed. "Sundarī Devī" refers to the goddess named Sundarī. "She succeeds" means she attains accomplishment (*siddhi*). By what? By the "mantra," namely the mantra that will be stated hereafter. How? "With true devotion," that is, by means of a particular excellence of sincere devotion.
The extraction of the mantra for propitiation: Oṃ sundari paramasundari svāhā.
One should write the word "Sundarī," beginning with Brahmā and ending with the word "Homa," within the pericarp;
and on all eight petals, one should write "Paramasundarī. (8.20)
Vivaraṇa:
"The word 'Brahmādisundarī' refers to the term *sundarī* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*; 'ending with *homa*' means ending with *svāhā*. 'In the center of the pericarp' refers to: *oṃ sundari svāhā*.

One should write [the mantra] within the pericarp. On all eight petals—that is, on the eight petals in the region outside that pericarp—one should write the term "Oṃ Paramasundarī Svāhā," writing it individually on each petal.
In a vessel made of clay from a potter’s hand, filled with oil of black sesame seeds,
[he should offer it] into a lamp produced from fire taken from a *nyagrodha* tree, using a wick made of lac.
*Vivaraṇa*:

"Filled with black sesame oil" means filled with oil produced from black sesame seeds. Furthermore, of what nature is it? "Made of clay from a potter's hand," meaning fashioned from clay held in the fingertips of a potter. In what? "In a vessel," that is, a lamp-vessel. "With a wick made of lac" means with a wick wrapped in a layer of lac. "In a lamp" means in a light. Of what nature is it? "Born from the fire of *nyagrodha* wood," meaning ignited by a fire produced from the wood of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*).
Having understood the eightfold worship of the virgin and so forth according to the previously stated procedure, it should be performed. This is for the purpose of the lamp.
Now the ritual procedure for the Ear-Demoness (Karṇapiśācī) is described:
"O Śravaṇapiśācinī, O Muṇḍā, svāhā!"—this mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), should be recited; it is perfected through one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpya*). || 8.22 ||
Vivaraṇa:

“O you who are a Piśācinī of the ear, O shaven-headed one” (*śravaṇapiśācini muṇḍe*) is the phrase. “Ending with *svāhā*” means having the word *svāhā* at its conclusion. Furthermore, of what nature is it? “To be recited preceded by the *praṇava*,” meaning it is uttered with the syllable *oṃ* as its beginning. “And it is perfected through a hundred thousand recitations” means that one attains success (*siddhi*) from a recitation numbering one hundred thousand. “This mantra is called Karṇapiśācī”—this mantra shall be known by the name Karṇapiśācī.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ śravaṇapiśācini muṇḍe svāhā.
Having smeared kuṣṭha consecrated with mantra upon the heart, face, ears, and pair of feet, one tells the intended matter to the ear-root of the sleeping person. (8.23)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Kuṣṭha consecrated with mantra” means kuṣṭha that has been empowered twenty-one times with the *Karṇapiśācinī* mantra and ground with water. “Having smeared the heart, face, ears, and pair of feet” means having applied this water-ground kuṣṭha to the heart, mouth, pair of ears, and pair of feet. “Of one who is asleep” means of one who is sleeping. “At the root of the ear” means at the base of the ear. “He speaks” means he says. “The task that was thought of” means whatever desired purpose [concerning] the past, future, or present.

One should write the seed-syllable (bīja) of the peak-mantra (kūṭa), endowed with the fourteenth kalā and the form of the letter *ma* (malayūṃ), situated within the circles of fire and wind, and placed upon a leaf of the *khara-tāḍa* tree together with the name. 8.24.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Endowed with *ma*, *la*, the syllable *yūṃ*, and the fourteenth vowel” means: *ma*, *la*, the syllable *yūṃ*, and the fourteenth vowel, which is *au*; “endowed with these” means surrounded by them—thus, “endowed with *ma*, *la*, the syllable *yūṃ*, and the fourteenth vowel. What is it? “The peak-seed-syllable,” that is, the seed-syllable *kṣa*. Thus, the seed-syllable is *kṣmlyūauṃ*. “One should write” means one should write this seed-syllable. How? “Situated within the mandalas of fire and wind,” meaning situated in the middle of the city of fire and the city of wind.
Furthermore, of what nature was it? It was "situated upon a palm-leaf bearing a name," meaning it rested on a palm-leaf inscribed with the name Devadatta.

By smearing the forehead with the milk of *mārtaṇḍa* and *snuhī*, along with the smoke produced from *trikaṭu*, *hayagandha*, and *sadmabhava*, one causes the house of householders to be entered by [the deity]. (8.25)

Vivaraṇa: ‘Mārtaṇḍasnuhidugdha’ means the milk of the *arka* (sun-plant) and the milk of the *snuhī* (thorn-apple). ‘Trikatu’ is well known. ‘Hayagandhā’ is *aśvagandhā*. ‘With the household-smokes’ means with the smoke from a house. Having ‘smeared’—that is, having smeared that leaf—with such substances as these; ‘situated on the forehead’ means situated on the brow. Of whom? ‘Of householders,’ that is, of married men. ‘It effects’ means it performs. What? ‘The entry into the house,’ that is, the descent into the home.
Having made a powder of realgar, sulphur, and talc, one should wrap it with white *arka* cotton and with a thread from a lotus stalk; thus a wick should be prepared here.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Kunaṭī’ is realgar (*manaḥśilā*); ‘gandhaka’ is well known; ‘tālaka’ is the powder of *godanta* (cow-tusk). ‘Having made [them]’ means having made a powder of these substances. ‘With white arka-cotton’ means with the cotton produced from the fruit of the white *arka* plant. ‘Having wrapped’ means having properly wrapped that powder within that cotton, and having further encircled it solely with ‘that lotus-stalk thread’—that is, with a thread produced from a lotus stalk. ‘A wick should be prepared here’ means that in this manner, a wick should be made here.
The practitioner should light a lamp with that [mixture] prepared with millet oil;
where the lamp goes face-down, there lies a heap of wealth.

*Vivaraṇa*: “That [wick] is to be saturated with *kaṅgu* oil”: that wick, once prepared, is to be soaked with *kaṅgu* oil. “With that”: with such a wick. “A lamp”: a lamp that has been lit. “One should awaken”: one should kindle. Who? “The practitioner” (*mantrī*), the reciter of mantras. “Where the lamp went face-down”: in whichever place that lamp goes with its flame downward; “there is a heap of wealth” (*vasurāśi*): it should be known that at that spot there is a heap of gold.

Reciting the mantra mentally, the practitioner of mantra should gaze at the lamp, which is the state of the wind and the end of space in the direction where the light of the Vinaya and other scriptures blazes forth. 8.28.
Commentary:

The phrase beginning with "vinayādi" and preceded by the syllable *oṃ* is "prajvalitajyotir diśāyām. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the "marunnabho'ntapada," accompanied by the word *svāhā*. "Reciting the mantra mentally" means uttering such a distinguished mantra with the mind. "The lamp" refers to an excellent light. "One should look upon" means one should gaze at it. Who? "The practitioner of mantra," the reciter of mantras.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ jvalitajyotir diśāyāṃ svāhā. This lamp-wick, having been ignited either on a horse's hoof or on a knife, should be established and observed.

Having combined the numbers of the planets beginning with the Sun (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), the mountains (7), the rivers (7), the misfortunes (9), the planets (9), and the nagas (8), and having added the number of the nails (20) and multiplied by three, one should divide again by the lunar days (15).
From the remainder, the wise man should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results, according to whether there is inequality or equality [in the sum].
This truth has been proclaimed here by the best of sages, who are like suns to the lotuses of those destined for liberation.

Vivaraṇa: “*Prāya*” is one name among the three types of people—children, youths, and the elderly; “*urvīśa*” is one name among universal sovereigns (*sārvabhauma*) kings; “*nadī*” is one name among great rivers such as the Gaṅgā; “*navagraha*” is one name among the nine planets beginning with the Sun; “*naga*” is one name among mountains such as Mandara; “*vyādhi*” is one name among diseases arising from wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*); and “*prasūna*” is one name among flowers such as the jasmine (*mallikā*), *jāti*, and the hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapatra*).”

‘Akṣarāṇi’: having combined the number of syllables spoken in the question from the beginning up to the end of the flowers; ‘ekīkṛtya’: having made all of those into a single numerical total; ‘nakhānvitam’: having added the number twenty to that sum of figures; ‘triguṇitam’: having multiplied that sum by three; ‘tithyā punar bhājitam’: then, subsequently, having divided the tripled sum by fifteen; ‘brūyāt’: one should state [the result].

Why? From the "remainder" (*uddharitāt*), that is, from what is left over after the portions have been subtracted. What is it? The "fruit of the auspicious and inauspicious" (*śubhāśubhaphalam*), meaning both the auspicious fruit and the inauspicious fruit. In what context? "In oddness and evenness" (*vaiṣamyasāmye*); one should declare an auspicious fruit for an odd number, and a contrary fruit for an even number. Who? The "wise one" (*sudhīḥ*), the intelligent person. "This is the truth" (*etattathyam*); this cause for inquiry is determined to be true. "Here" (*iha*), in this system (*kalpe*). "It was declared" (*uditam*), explained. By whom? By the "best of sages" (*munivaraiḥ*), the bulls among sages.

By what kind [of beings]? By those who are like the sun to the lotuses of the worthy (bhavya); that is, by those sages who act as the sun to the very lotuses that are the worthy ones—this is the question.
Having correctly drawn a trident with its tip reaching the crescent moon-line in the center, the wise one [should do so] on that lunar day—
either the new moon or the first day of the fortnight— on which the moon remains stationed.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Situated at the tip of the crescent-line” means situated at the tip of the line shaped like a half-moon. What is that? It is the “trident,” having the form of a trident; it is not merely a trident situated at the tip of a line shaped like a full moon. “And in the middle”: the trident is also [to be drawn] in the middle of that line shaped like a half-moon. “Having properly inscribed”: having written it beautifully and with excellence. Who? “The wise one,” the intelligent one. “In the lunar mansion” (*ṛkṣe*): in a constellation. “But on the day of the new moon and the first day” (*amāvāsyāpratipaddine tu*): on the day of the first day (*pratipad*) as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is concluding.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on which asterism the moon, that bearer of the deer-mark, ‘remains’—that is, stays fixed—is [the one in question].
Taking that as the starting point and counting through the positions in battle, one should know that death occurs when [the planet] reaches the tip of the trident;
victory occurs at those numbered with the sun (twelve); and defeat occurs when it stands outside those six.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Having made that the beginning” means: on the day of its commencement, having placed that lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in which the moon resides at the tip of the trident line, one takes that lunar mansion as the starting point. “Having counted”: where? “In battle”; one should count until the day in the battle when the birth lunar mansion of the fighting person is reached. “Death among those situated at the tip of the trident”: when the birth lunar mansion comes to be situated at the tip of the trident, then death occurs.

One should know (*vindyet*): "and victory among those numbered as Mārtaṇḍas" means that victory occurs among those twelve asterisms situated within the lines shaped like a half-moon; "defeat in the six situated outside" means that defeat occurs among the six asterisms situated outside the lines shaped like a half-moon.
Thus ends the section on battle concerning the diagram of the crescent moon line.
In every direction and intermediate direction, let the minister grant [the desired object] to the querent from those situated between both;
sequentially, for a boy, a girl, a eunuch, and for one with a full womb. (8.32)
Vivaraṇa:

"In every direction and intermediate direction" means in the cardinal and intermediate points. "By those situated between those two" means by those situated on both sides of those two—the cardinal and intermediate directions—referring to those standing on both flanks. "May he grant" means may he declare. "To the questioner" means to the person who asks the question. Who? "The counselor," that is, the practitioner of mantra. How? "Successively," that is, in due order.

"A boy, a girl, or a neuter": if the questioner asks regarding a direction, he should indicate a boy; if the questioner asks regarding an intermediate direction (vidiś), he should indicate a girl; and if the questioner stands between the direction and the intermediate direction, he should indicate a neuter. Of whom? "Of one with a full womb," that is, of one who is fully pregnant.
Having combined the letters and measures of the husband and wife and divided them by three,
one should indicate the clay man by zero and the woman by two. (8.33)
Vivaraṇa:

"And the letters and measures" (*varṇamātrāś ca*): the letters (*varṇāḥ*) range from *ka* to *ha*, and the measures (*mātrāḥ*) are the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. Of whom? "Of the couple" (*dampatyoḥ*), i.e., of the woman and the man. "Having unified" (*ekīkṛtya*): having separated the letters and measures of their names individually, one places them all in a single location. "Divided by three" (*tribhājitāḥ*): that heap is divided by the number three. "By zero and one" (*śūnyenaikena*): by the zero remaining after that division and by one. "Death of the man" (*mṛtpuṃsaḥ*): the death of the male.
"By two fingers less than that for a woman," meaning by two fingers less than that [measurement] for a woman, one "should indicate"—that is, should declare—the death of the woman.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the section on omens, in the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa* composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri, the crest-jewel of poets in both languages. 8.
The ninth chapter: On medicinal herbs for subjugating women and others. || 9 ||
Clove, saffron, ushira root, nagakesara, black mustard,
cardamom, realgar, costus, tagara, blue lotus, and gorochana.

*Vivaraṇa*: ‘Lavaṅga’ is *devakusuma*; ‘kuṅkuma’ is *vālhīka*; ‘uśīra’ is white *vālaka*; ‘nāgakesara’ is *cāmpeya*; ‘rājikāḥ’ are white mustard seeds; ‘elā’ is *pṛthvīkā*; ‘manaḥśilā’ is *kunaṭī*; ‘kuṣṭha’ is *vāpya*; ‘tagara’ is *piṇḍītagara*; ‘utpala’ is the white lotus; ‘rocanā’ is *piṅgalā*.
Having taken equal parts of śrīkhaṇḍa, tulasī, pippalī, padmaka, and kuṭaja, under the lunar mansion named Puṣya, one should proceed.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Śrīkhaṇḍa’ is sandalwood derived from the *mākha* tree; ‘tulasī’ is the fragrant basil; ‘pikvī’ is a fragrant substance; ‘padmaka’ is well known; ‘kuṭajānvita’ means accompanied by *indrayava* (seeds of *Holarrhena*). ‘Having taken all in equal measure’ means having taken all these in equal portions; ‘under the asterism named Puṣya’ means under the asterism called Puṣya.
A maiden should grind everything with water as cold as ice;
when the moon has risen, apply this *tilaka* which fascinates all people.

Vivaraṇa: “By a maiden” means by a young girl. “One should grind” means one should pulverize. “All” refers to all that medicinal substance. By what? “By water produced from snow,” that is, by water born from frost. “Prepare it. Where? “When the rising of the moon has occurred,” that is, when the emergence of nectar has occurred. What? “A tilaka,” a sectarian mark. Of what nature? “Deluding people,” meaning it brings people under one’s control.
The excrement of the *barhiśikhā*, *asitaguñjā*, *gorambhā*, and *bhānukīṭaka*, combined with one's own five impurities, when made into a powder, brings a woman under one's control. (9.4)
Commentary:

‘Barhiśikhā’ is peacock’s crest; ‘sitaguñjā’ is white guñjā; ‘gorambhā’ is well-known. ‘Bhānukīṭakasya malam’ is the excrement of the insect found on *arka* leaves. ‘Nijapañcamalopetam’ means combined with its own five impurities. ‘Cūrṇam’ refers to betel-leaf powder mixed with these substances. ‘Vanitām’ means a woman. ‘Vaśīkurute’ means he brings her under his control.
Having prepared many pills from karavīra, bhujaṅgākṣī, jārī, daṇḍī, indravāruṇī, gobandhinī, and salajjā— 9.5.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Karavīra’ is the root of *raktāśvamāra*; ‘bhujaṅgākṣī’ is the root of *sarpākṣī*; ‘jārī’ is *putrañjārī*; ‘daṇḍī’ is the root of *brahmadaṇḍī*; ‘indravāruṇī’ is the root of *viśālā*; ‘gobandhinī’ is *adhaḥpuṣpī*, though some say it is *priyaṅgu*. Having ground the powder of these substances—‘of the modest ones,’ meaning those possessed of roots on all sides—and having prepared many pills (*vaṭikā*).
Having mixed salt with pills and cooked them in one's own urine within a clean vessel, one should administer it in food; this is a means of enchanting women. (9.6)
Vivaraṇa:

"Having thrown it together with the pills" means having cast it together with the pills under discussion; that is, having mixed it. What? "Salt," namely sea salt. Where? "In a beautiful vessel," that is, in a pleasing container. "Having cooked it" means having performed the process of boiling. How? "With its own urine," that is, with one's own urine. "One should give it in food" means one should add it to rice and other such items. It will become "a deluder of women," meaning it will bewitch female folk.
Having placed a white guñjā seed together with a *lajjārikā* plant inside the mouth of a dead snake,
and having mixed them with the hair from the matted locks of a *rudra*, one should draw [the substance] for a period of three days.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“In the midst of the mouth of a dead serpent” means in the middle of the mouth of a black snake that has reached its end (death). “*Lajjarikā*” is the root of *samaṅgā*. “Having placed” means having properly deposited. “White *guñjā*” is white *raktikā*. Of what kind is it? “Mixed with *rudrajaṭā*” means conjoined with *rudrajaṭā*. “Having drawn out for three days” means having kept these three roots within the mouth of that serpent for three days, and afterwards, “having drawn out,” meaning having extracted them.
One should sprinkle the powder of *lāṅgalikā* tubers over ground smeared with cow dung,
having infused it with dog’s milk and the excrement produced from its five limbs.
Vivaraṇa:

"In the tuber of the lāṅgalikā" means having excavated the tuber of the kali-hārī plant, one should place it between two joined vessels. In what state? "Smeared with cow dung," meaning having coated it thoroughly with dried cow dung. "One should scatter the powder" means one should deposit the powder made from the three previously mentioned medicinal herbs into the middle of that tuber. Having done what? "Having infused," meaning having properly saturated that powder. With what? "With the milk of a female dog," that is, with the milk of a black female dog; it should not be infused with the milk of just any dog.
‘Having also meditated upon it with one’s own impurities produced from the five limbs,’ that is, even by means of the impurities generated from one's own five limbs.
The impurities of the eyes and ears, semen, and likewise the impurities of the teeth and tongue—
these five types of impurity are said by those who know mantras to be used for the rite of subjugation (vaśyakarman).
*Vivaraṇa*:

"Eye" (*netram*) means the organ of sight; "ear" (*śrotram*) means the organ of hearing; the "impurity" (*malam*) is that of these two. "Semen" (*śukram*) is the seed. "Tooth" (*dantaḥ*) means a tusk; "tongue" (*jihvā*) means the organ of taste; the "impurity" is that of these two. "In that manner" (*tathā*) means by that method. "In the rite of subjugation" (*vaśyakarmaṇi*) refers to performing the rite for bringing women under one's control. "By those who know the mantras" (*mantrajñaiḥ*) means by those who are learned in the mantras. "The five-limbed impurity is spoken of" (*pañcāṅgamalam ucyate*) means it is thus described as the five-limbed impurity.
Having cooked this powder, it then becomes a supreme means for bringing the world under one's control;
one should add it to food and drink for both men and women to consume together.

Vivaraṇa: ‘Having cooked’ (paktvā) means having performed the act of cooking. ‘This powder’ (cūrṇam idam) refers to this aforementioned powder. ‘Afterwards’ (paścāt) means immediately following that. ‘Bringing the world under control’ (jagadvaśyakaraṃ) means bringing all people under one's power. ‘Supremely’ (paraṃ) means to the highest degree. ‘One should give’ (dadyāt) means let one give. To what? ‘In foods and drinks’ (khādyānnapāneṣu), that is, in things to be eaten and drunk. Of whom? ‘Of both woman and man’ (strīpuṃsoś ca), that is, of the female and the male. How? ‘Mutually’ (parasparaṃ); one should give it to each other, and thus they become submissive.
Having been processed with the juice of the five milky trees and the juice of the *potakyaṇḍaka* plant, a wick for a sesame oil lamp becomes the deluder of the people of the three worlds. 9.11.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“With the milk of the five trees” refers to the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭī*; some say that in place of *vaṭa*, one should use *vaṃdula*. Thus, it means with the milks of these five milk-yielding trees. Not only with the milks of the five milk-yielding trees, but also “with the juice of the *potavayaṇḍaka*,” which is the juice of the black *manthelikā*. “The wick for the five-threaded lamp” should be soaked; it is made of five types of threads: *arkatūla*, lotus fiber, *sālmalītūla*, *paṭṭa*, and cotton (*kapāsa*). “The wick for the sesame-oil lamp.”
"She becomes the deluder of the people of the three worlds" means she becomes the cause of delusion for those residing in the three worlds.
A powder of *viṣamuṣṭika*, *kanaka*, *halinī*, and *piśācikā*, mixed with water from the body and placed in a vessel of a madman, brings the betel nut (*kramuka*) under one's control. || 9.12 ||

*Vivaraṇa*: “*Viṣamuṣṭiḥ*” is *viṣadoḍikā*; “*kanakam*” is black dhattūra; “*halinī*” is *kalihalinī*; “*piśācikā*” is *kapikacchukā*. “*Cūrṇam*” is the powder of these four substances. “*Ambu dehabhavam*” is one’s own urine. “*Unmattakabhāṇḍagatam*” means this powder of the substances, together with one’s own urine, is kept for three days inside a vessel made from the fruit of the black dhattūra. “*Kramukaphalam*” is the areca nut (*pūgīphala*).
“*Tadvaśaṃ kurute*” means that when that areca nut is given to be chewed, it brings the woman under one's control.
Having taken a betel nut placed in the mouth and collected it after three days, one should reduce each of these with the powders of *kanaka*, *viṣamuṣṭi*, and *halinī*. (9.13)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“*Kramukaphalam*” means the areca nut (*pūgīphala*). “*Mukhanihitam*” means placed in the mouth of a serpent. “*Tasmāt*” means from that serpent’s mouth. “*Divasatrayeṇa saṃgṛhya*” means having taken that areca nut after three days have passed. “*Kanaka-viṣamuṣṭi-halinī-cūrṇaiḥ*” refers to the powder of the root of *dhattūra*, the powder of *viṣadoḍikā*, and the powder of *halinī*; “*pratyekam*” means each separately; “*saṃkṣipya (pya)*” means having added [them].

Having sequentially infused *madana* and betel nut with the milk of a she-ass, a mare, and a female dog, one should add them to food; this is declared to be a means of bringing women under one's control. 9.14.
Vivaraṇa:

“With the milks of the donkey, horse, and bitch” means with the milks of the ass, horse, and female dog. “Successively” (kramaśaḥ) means in order. “Having infused” (paribhāvya) means it should be processed; the gold powder is to be infused with donkey’s milk, the *viṣamuṣṭi* powder with horse’s milk, and the *halinī* powder with the bitch’s milk—thus, in that sequence, that betel nut (*pūgīphala*) is to be infused over three days. “One should add to the food” (*yojayet khādye*): this betel nut, perfected by this method, should be added entirely to the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*).
‘Madanakramuka’ is that which brings women under one's control; it is a betel nut known by the name Anaṅgabāṇa. ‘Samuddiṣṭaḥ’ means correctly described.
Putrañjārī, kuṅkuma, śarapuṅkhī, mohanī, śamī, kuṣṭha, gorocanā, hikesara, tagara, rudantī, and karpūra. 9.15.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Puttañjarī’ is well-known; ‘kuṅkuma’ is from Kāśmīra; ‘śarapuṅkhī’ is the white arrow-leaf plant; ‘mohanī’ is the *vaṭapatrikā*; ‘śamī’ is the hair-destroyer; ‘kuṣṭa’ is *koṣṭha*. ‘Gorocanā’ is the tawny pigment; ‘ahikesara’ is *nāgakesara*; ‘tagara’ is *piṇḍītagara*; ‘rudantī’ is well-known. ‘Karpūra’ is that which is joined with the moon (*candrānvita*).
Having made a powder of these and having then thrown it into the midst of the barley-gruel,
a wick should again be prepared from that, encased in a lotus-fiber thread.
Vivaraṇa:

"Of these aforementioned substances," *having made a powder* means having prepared a powder. "Then, having cast it into the midst of lac" means immediately thereafter, having placed that powder into the middle of a layer of lac. "Encircled by a lotus-fiber wick" means encircled by a thread produced from a lotus stalk. "A wick should be made" means a wick should be fashioned in this manner. "Again, with that" means subsequently, with that which is about to be described.
Having infused it with the milk flowing from the breasts of women of the three castes,
and then with the milk from the udders of artisan women, one should subsequently awaken the lamp with the ghee of a tawny cow.
Vivaraṇa:

“With the milk produced from the breasts of five artisans” means with the milk arising from the breasts of the five types of artisan women. “With the breast-milk flowing from women of the three castes” means, after that milk from the breasts of artisan women, with the breast-milk of women belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya classes. “Having infused” means the previously prepared wick should be saturated with those milks. “Then,” after the infusion, “with the ghee of a Kapila cow,” that is, with the clarified butter of a Kapila cow. “One should awaken” means one should ignite. What? “The lamp.”

When both [the lunar mansions] are present, during the Festival of Lights, collyrium should be applied in a new earthen bowl while standing on ground smeared with cow dung that has been consecrated by mantras. 9.18.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“During both eclipses” means during the eclipses of the moon and the sun. “And during the festival of lamps” means, alternatively, on the occasion of the Dīpāvalī festival. “Collyrium should be applied in a new earthen bowl” means that collyrium—specifically soot—should be taken in a fresh vessel made of clay. “On ground smeared with cow dung” means on earth that has been swept clean with cow dung that has not fallen from a cow. “Having stayed” means having remained there. On what kind of ground? “On ground consecrated by mantras,” meaning on ground sprinkled with the mantra that will be described hereafter.

The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ bhūr bhūmidevate tiṣṭha tiṣṭha ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ. This is the mantra for sweeping the ground. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Candraprabha, who is honored by Candra and Indra, whose eyes are enchanting; O Hariṇi, Hariṇi, bring everything under control, bring it under control! Svāhā. This is the mantra for extracting collyrium. Oṃ, homage to the Being, to the composed one, to Kāma, to Rāma; Oṃ culu culu, gulu gulu, O blue bee, O blue bee, O heart-stealer, homage! This is the mantra for [the application of] collyrium.
The mantra for eye-collyrium.
Seeing her with eyes colored by collyrium, even Madana desires her here;
even for a man whose eyes are anointed [with it], kings and others fall under his control. (9.19)
Commentary:

“With eyes colored by collyrium” (*kajjalarañjitanayane*) means eyes anointed with collyrium. “Having seen” (*dṛṣṭvā*) means having beheld. “Her”—the beloved woman—“even Madana here desires,” meaning even Kāmadeva comes under her control. “Even seeing a man whose eyes are anointed,” [it follows that] “kings and others come under his power”; that is, from the collyrium-anointed man, the Kṣatriyas and others become submissive due to that ointment.

Then, the root of *viṣamuṣṭi* and *kanaka*, ground with resin, lac, and water, and having its leaves impregnated with that juice, causes one to become possessed by a *piśāca* once it has entered the middle of the stomach. 9.20.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“*Viṣamuṣṭiḥ*” means *viṣadoḍikā*. “*Kanakamūlam*” means the root of the *dhattūra* plant. “*With water containing *rālākṣata*” means with water washed with *rālākṣata*. “*Ground from that*” means ground from that [root]. “*A betel leaf impregnated with its juice*” means a betel leaf saturated with the juice of that ground medicinal herb. “*Acts like a *piśāca*” means it behaves like a *piśāca*. “*Having entered the middle of the belly*” means when it has reached the interior of the stomach, it turns the person into a *piśāca*.
In a mother’s house, upon a human skull smeared with fresh ink from a Piśācī desiring a smooth surface, using a wick made of forest cotton— || 9.21 ||
*Vivaraṇa*:

‘Cikkaṇikā’ means *iloṭhā*, known in the Karṇāṭaka language as *uhāṭhā*. ‘Īpsitarūpā’ means multiform, specifically the female lizard (*saraṭaviṭ*). ‘Piśācikā’ refers to the *kapikacchū* plant. ‘In that which is churned with ink produced from fresh cow-dung’ means in that which is stirred by ink originating from fresh cow-dung. Where? ‘In a human skull,’ that is, in a skull-bowl. ‘In a temple of the Mothers’ means in the abode of the Seven Mothers (*saptamātṛkāḥ*). ‘With a wick made of wild cotton’ means with a wick fashioned from the cotton-wool found in the forest.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, this collyrium produced from great clarified butter should be kept;
with it, one may also prepare a trident as collyrium for the purpose of warding off the fear of marks.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“To be held” (*dhāryam*) means it should be carried. “On the eighth day of the dark fortnight” (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamyām*) means on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. What is it? “Collyrium” (*añjanam*), that is, lampblack. “This” refers to this collyrium. “Produced from great ghee” (*mahāghṛtodbhūtam*) means originating from excellent clarified butter. “With that one should fashion a trident” (*triśūlaṃ kuryāt*): by means of the collyrium prepared in this manner, one should fashion not only a trident. “One should also make collyrium for the eyes” (*añjanam api kuryāt*): let him also prepare eye-salve.
For what purpose? “For the sake of causing fear through the mark” (*aṅkabhītyartham*): this collyrium is for the purpose of instilling fear in the adversary.

The mantra for extracting that collyrium is as follows: *Oṃ namo bhagavati hiḍimbavāsini allallamāṃsappiye nahayalamaṇḍalapaïṭṭhie tuha raṇamatte paharaṇaduṭṭhe āyāsamaṇḍi pāyālamaṇḍi siddhamaṇḍi joiṇimaṇḍi savvamuhamaṇḍi kajjalaṃ paḍaü svāhā*. This is a Prākṛt mantra. The application of the collyrium should be performed while facing the northeast (*aiśānī*).
Having collected the soot from the branches of the Yama-tree— the tree of the elements burnt by the fire of consciousness—
one should also take Aṅkolla oil, mercury, black Biḍālī, and the placenta.
Vivaraṇa:

"The soot from the branches of the tree of the Kali age burnt by the fire of the funeral pyre" means the soot produced from the branches of the tree of the Kali age ignited by the funeral pyre, originating from the southern direction. "Having gathered" means having properly collected. "Aṅkolla oil" is the oil produced from the seeds of the aṅkolla plant. "Sūtaka" is mercury (pāradarasa). "And the placenta of a black cat" refers also to the placenta of a black female cat.
Having made a pill from the eye-fluid of an owl, compounded with the three metals, and having placed it in his own mouth, a man becomes invisible. 9.24.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Having made a pill from the water of an owl’s eye rubbed together” means having made a pill from four substances, such as ink produced from the *bhūtadruma* tree, which have been rubbed with the water of an owl’s eye. “Encased in three metals” means having thoroughly ground it with the three metals known as copper, silver, and gold, in proportions consisting of twelve, sixteen, and three parts respectively. “Holding it in his own mouth” means holding that pill, encased in the three metals, within his own mouth. “The man” refers to the person. “Invisibility” means the state of being unseen.
“He attains” means he comes to possess it.
Having taken the root of the white *śarapuṅkha* and white *kokilākṣa* seeds,
ground with the juice of *vanavasala*, it causes the immobilization of semen when placed in the mouth. (9.25)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“The root of the *sitaśarapuṅkha*” means the root of the white *bāṇapuṅkha*. “Having taken” means having grasped. “And the seeds of the white *kokilākṣa*” means the seeds of the white *kokilākṣa*. “Ground with the juice of wild *vasalā*” means ground with the juice of the forest-born (*vana*) *upodakī*; *vanavalā* is *kāsali* in the Karṇāṭaka language. “Arresting the virility” means the arrest of semen. “Situated in the mouth” means situated in the mouth of the man.
Having taken a fragment of a scorpion from the right shank of a black cat and binding it around the waist region, it causes the suppression of semen in men. (9.26)
Vivaraṇa:

"Of the right shank of a black cat" means of the right shank of a black *biḍāla* (wildcat). "A fragment of bone" refers to a piece of that [cat's] bone. "Having taken" means having seized it. "Bound to the waist region" means bound to the waist region of a man. "Of men" means of human beings. It "produces" or effects the paralysis of virility (*vīryastambha*).
A lamp kindled with the ghee of a tawny cow, combined with the powder of cochineal insects, arrests male virility at the onset of sexual union during the night. 9.27.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“With *kapilā* ghee” means with tawny clarified butter (*kapilājya*). “A lamp awakened” means a lamp set ablaze. Of what nature is it? It is “mixed with the powder of *suragopa*,” meaning provided with a wick made from the interior of the powder of the *indragopa* insect. What does that lamp do? He says: “It paralyzes” (*stambhayati*), i.e., it effects paralysis. What? “Manly vigor” (*puruṣavīrya*), i.e., human virility. Where? “At the onset of passion” (*ratyārambhe*), i.e., at the beginning of sexual union. When? “At the time of night” (*niśāsamaye*), i.e., during the night.
Having applied a paste made of borax, long pepper, māsūra beans, camphor, and the juice of *mātuliṅga* to one's own fingers, one causes the vulva of women to flow. 9.28.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Ṭaṅkaṇa’ is that which grows on the banks of the Mālatī; ‘pippalikāmā’ is the Mahārāṣṭrī plant; ‘sūraṇa’ is the white wild sūraṇa tuber; ‘karpūra’ is camphor; ‘mātuliṅga’ is the citron (bījapūra). By means of their juices, having made an ‘application to one’s own fingers,’ that is, an application to one’s own fingers, it causes the ‘melting of the vulva,’ that is, the flowing from the vulva, of women—that is, of wives.

The root of the white Apāmārga plant, situated in the direction of Kubera (the north), should be taken from the three northern [nodes]; that which is located at the head is won through gambling and debate.

Commentary: “The root of the white apāmārga” means the root of the white *kharamañjarī*. Of what nature is it? “Situated in the direction of Kubera,” that is, in the north. “In the triad of the Uttarās” refers to the three lunar mansions: Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, and Uttarā-bhādrapadā. “To be taken” means it should be gathered. “Located on the head” means situated upon the crown of the head. “Victorious in gambling and debate” means it brings victory in dice games and in disputes.
One should place double that amount of *haravīrya* into a snake turned by fire; it should then be rubbed together with *munika*, gold, *nāga*, *sarpa*, *jyotiṣmatī*, and *atasī*.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“In the serpent turned by fire” means in the serpent processed by fire. “The virility of Hara” is mercury (*pāradarasa*). “Then one should add double that” means one should add two parts of mercury from that single part of the serpent. “The Sage” is *raktāgasti*. “Gold” is black thorn-apple (*kṛṣṇadhattūra*). “Serpent-creeper” is *nāgadamanaka*. “And with *jyotiṣmatī* and *atasī*” means with *kaṅguṇī* and *atasī*. “That should be rubbed” means that aforementioned serpent should be ground with the juices of these.
Having ground it with ḍīka and fashioned it into a love-bracelet for a courtesan, one should cause the destruction of the pride of passion in women at the time of sexual union. 9.31.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“With *ḍīka* resin”—that is, with the exudation. “Having rubbed”—having performed the rubbing once again. Of what [tree]’s *ḍīka*? Of the *gaṇiyārī*, the *karṇikāra* tree. “Having made a ring of passion”—having placed a ring of *smara* upon the penis. “At the time of pleasure”—during sexual union. “Of women”—of females. “The destroyer of the pride of pleasure”—the destroyer of the arrogance of sexual enjoyment. “He should make”—he performs it.
The juice of *vyāghrī* and *bṛhatī* fruits, *sūraṇa* tubers, *kaṇḍūtī*, and water from *caṇaka* leaves;
the powder of *kapikacchu*, *vajravallī*, *pippalī*, and *āmalakī*. 9.32.

Commentary: ‘The juice of *vyāghrī* and *bṛhatī* fruits’ means the juice of the fruits of the two types of *bṛhatī*. ‘*Sūraṇa*’ refers to white *sūraṇa*. ‘*Kaṇḍūti*’ is *agnika*. ‘Water from *caṇaka* leaves’ is water from fresh *caṇaka* leaves. ‘*Kapikacchu*’ is *piśācikā*. ‘*Vajravallī*’ is *kāṇḍavallī*. ‘*Pippalikāmā*’ is *mahārāṣṭrī*. ‘*Amlikā*’ is *cāṅgerī*. ‘Powder’ (*cūrṇa*) refers to the juice of some [of these].
One should meditate nine times upon the serpent Agnyāvartita with these substances;
by thus forming the "Smara-ring," one brings about the melting of women.
Vivaraṇa:

"A nāga coiled around fire" means nine times; "one should meditate" means one should perform the visualization. By what means? "By these substances," that is, by the substances mentioned here. "Having thus made a ring of passion" means having fashioned a ring of *madana* (love) in this manner. "Of women" means of females. "Melting" means the flowing forth from the *bhaga*. "He effects" means he performs it.

One should perform the purification using dinārs obtained from a newborn child whose number corresponds to the count of the sun’s rays (twelve thousand), along with the juice of *aṅkola* trees, kings, and *vṛkṣakumārī*. 9.34.
Vivaraṇa:

“The number twelve, sixteen, and twenty-four” refers to these three numbers. “Dīnāras taken according to the measure prescribed in the Sūta[ka]” means the *gadyāṇakas* of mercury (*pāradarasa*) taken according to the measures stated in those three [numbers]. “One should perform the purification of the juices of *aṅkolla*, *rājavṛkṣa*, and *kumārī*”: “the juice of *aṅkolla*” is the juice of *sampāka*; “the juice of *rājavṛkṣa*” [is as stated]; “the juice of *kumārī*” is the juice of *gṛhakanyā*. One should perform the purification of the mercury with these juices.
One should rub the mercury for twenty-one days with the powders of śaśirekhā, kharakarṇī, kokila, nayanā, apamārga, and kanaka. 9.35.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Śaśirekhā” is the seed of *vākucī*; “kharakaṇī” is *gardabhakarṇī*, known in the Karṇāṭaka language as *kartyegiri*; “kokilānayana” is the seed of *kokilākṣi*; “apāmārga” is the seed of *pratyekapuṣpī*; and “kanaka” is black datura (*kṛṣṇadhattūra*). “Together with the powders for twenty-one days” means that for each of these powders, one should rub [the substance] for twenty-one days. “One should rub the mercury” means one should rub purified quicksilver (*rasa*).
At night, having offered incense of sour gruel, one should insert it into the womb,
having recognized whether the woman is young, middle-aged, or nearing the end of her life, according to that sequence. (9.36)
*Vivaraṇa*:

"At night" means during the night. "Having given *kāñjikā*-incense" means having given incense made from fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*). "One should insert it into the womb" means one should insert that incensed substance into the female womb. "Having recognized the woman as young, middle-aged, or past her prime, according to that sequence": having understood the sequence—that for young women, a leech (*jalūkā*) made of a substance weighing twelve *gadyāṇas* is used; for women of middle stature, a leech made of a substance weighing sixteen *gadyāṇas*; and for women who have mostly passed their youth, a leech made of a substance weighing twenty-four *gadyāṇas*—one should insert it accordingly.
Even a woman who has become despondent in the battle of love, though she be intoxicated with passion—
such a one as this too he causes to melt by the application of leeches.
Vivaraṇa:

"Bearing a state of saplessness" means maintaining a condition of being devoid of fluidity. "A woman" (yoṣā) means a female. "In the battle of passion" (ratisaṃgare) means on the battlefield of sexual union. "Intoxicated with pride" means intoxicated by the pride of youth. "He causes even such a one to flow" means he causes even one who is thus intoxicated with pride to discharge [her fluids]. "But this application of leeches" (jalūkāprayoga)—that is to say, furthermore, this—refers to the application of leeches performed according to the method described above. Thus ends the rule for the application of leeches.
The root of *kapikacchu* growing at the foot of a *soma* tree, ground with cow’s urine, causes a *śākinī* to see the reflection of her own forehead-mark upon the head of another *śākinī*. (9.38)
Vivaraṇa:

"Having its root situated in the north" means having its root directed toward the northern direction. Of what? Of the *kapikacchu*, the female piśāca. Of what nature is the root? "Ground with cow-water," that is, processed with cow-urine. "The reflection of her own tilaka" means the likeness of her own cosmetic mark. "She beholds it upon the head of the śākinī" means she sees that very same tilaka of hers on the forehead of the śākinī.

In the ritual for the divine pillar of unbroken rice and *āditya*, the wise man should consume black pepper and long pepper; in the case of the divine pillar, he should also eat powdered ginger. 9.39.
Vivaraṇa:

Regarding “in the rite of the divine pillar of the sun’s grain” (*ādityākṣatadivyastambhavidhau*), it means in the procedure for the divine pillar of *āditya*-rice. Regarding “of black pepper and long pepper” (*maricapippalīkām*), one should consume the powder of black pepper and *mahārāṣṭrī*. However, for the divine pillar of camphor, [one uses] a skull-cup (*kapālikā*) and so forth, or a potsherd (*karpara*) and so forth. Regarding “in the divine pillar” (*divyastambhe*), it means in the performance of the divine pillar rite. “And one should consume the powder of ginger” (*suṇṭhīcūrṇaṃ ca bhakṣayet*) means one should consume the powder of the great medicinal herb (*mahauṣadhī*). Who? “The wise one” (*dhīmān*), that is, the intelligent person.
The fat of a female frog smeared on the hand causes the suppression of fire;
by the restraint of the breath, the suspension of the ordeal by scales and the like certainly occurs.
*Vivaraṇa*:

‘Lajjarikā’ means one possessed of a *lajjarikā* (a type of plant). ‘Bhekavasā’ means the fat of a frog. ‘Karaliptam’ means the hands smeared with the powder of that [plant] and its fat. ‘It effects the immobilization of fire’ means that the suppression of fire certainly occurs. ‘By the cessation of breath, the immobilization of the balance-divine ordeal and so forth occurs’ means that by the cessation of breath, the immobilization of the balance-divine ordeal (*tulādivya*) in the jar certainly and inevitably occurs.
If *nirguṇḍikā* and *siddhārthā* are tied at the door of a house or in a marketplace during the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun, buying and selling will take place. (9.41)

Commentary: ‘Nirguṇḍikā’ is *sitabhūtakeśī*. ‘Siddhārthāḥ’ are white mustard seeds. ‘At the house door’ means at the door of one’s own residence; ‘or in the market’ means in the marketplace. ‘Bound during the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun’ means if it is bound during the yoga of the Puṣya asterism on a Sunday. ‘Trade arises’ means that the buying and selling of goods certainly takes place.
If she drinks the *japā* flower after crushing it with sour gruel during the flowering season, she will not conceive; even if she consumes ghee, no embryo shall be formed within her. (9.42)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“She drinks” means she consumes it. “At the time of the flower” means during the period when flowers bloom for three days. What [does she drink]? “The *japā* flower,” that is, the *japā* blossom. Having done what? “Having crushed it thoroughly,” that is, having ground it well. With what? “With sour gruel (*kañjika*),” that is, with fermented rice water. “She,” meaning the woman; “the flower,” meaning the blossom; “does not bear,” meaning she does not retain it.
“Even if retained”: even if by some means she should retain the flower, nevertheless, “she would have no pregnancy”—there is simply no occurrence of conception for that woman.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Section on the Ritual for Subjugation," in the *Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa* composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇasūri, the crest-jewel of poets in both languages. 9.
The tenth chapter: The Section on the Gāruḍa Tantra. || 10 ||
I shall now describe the gathering [of the deities], the placement of the limbs, protection, the ritual of stobha, and the rite for paralyzing;
as well as the destruction of poison, the incitement [of spirits], and the treatment of bites from chalk-dust, hooded snakes, and other fanged creatures. 10.1.

*Vivaraṇa*: “*Saṃgrahaṃ*” means the gathering [of the venom] from the bitten person. “*Aṅganyāsaṃ*” means the arrangement of syllables upon the body of the bitten person. “*Rakṣāṃ*” means performing protection for the bitten person. “*Stobhaṃ ca*” means causing the entry [of the poison] into the bitten person; *ca* is used as a conjunction. “*Vacmy ahaṃ*” means I, the master Malliṣeṇa, speak. “*Stambhaṃ*” means the obstruction of the spreading of poison within the body of the bitten person. “*Viṣanāśanaṃ*” means the neutralization of the poison.

“Sacodyam” means that which exists together with a challenge (codya); it refers to curiosities such as the covering of a cloth bitten by a snake. “And the bite of a chalk-drawn serpent’s fang”—the connection is that I shall speak of this eightfold Gāruḍa concerning the bite of a serpent’s fang drawn in chalk.
First, the summary is stated:

When the messenger speaks with an equal or uneven number of syllables, and when the moon and sun are both waxing—if the messenger is thus, one should know that the bitten person will live; if the opposite, death. (10.2) cf. *Yogaratnāvalī* 1.37.
Vivaraṇa:

"When the messenger speaks with an equal number of syllables, the moon and sun are both moving [favorably]"; that is, the moon and sun are both in operation as the respective sounds. "There is life for the bitten one": when the messenger speaks with an equal number of syllables and the moon is moving, and when the messenger speaks with an unequal number of syllables and the sun is moving, one should know that there is a chance of survival for the person who has been bitten.

"One should know that for one bitten [by a snake], there is life if [the messenger] speaks with an even number of syllables while the Sun is in transit, but death if [the messenger] speaks with an odd number of syllables while the Moon is in transit. Thus, when there is a discrepancy between the vowels and consonants [of the messenger's speech], one should know that there is no recovery for the bitten person.
Having doubled the syllables arising from the mouth of the messenger, one should divide them by three;
with the remainder being zero, the wise man should predict death or life. 10.3.
Vivaraṇa:

“Having doubled the syllables arising from the mouth of the messenger”—meaning, having doubled all those interrogative syllables; “one should divide by three”—one should divide that doubled heap by three; “and by the remainder being zero”—by that remainder of the division being zero, which is a division by one (an even divisor), and by [the remainder] being one or two; “one should declare death or life”—if the remainder is zero, one should declare the absence of recovery for the one bitten; if the remainder is one or two, one should declare that there is recovery for the one bitten.

If one sprinkles the body of someone with water consecrated by the mantra *haṃ vaṃ kṣaṃ*, that person will live; otherwise, if bitten, they will not survive, except in the case of a twitching of the eye. (10.4) cf. Yogaratnāvalī 1.44–45.
Vivaraṇa:

The mantra is *haṃ vaṃ kṣaṃ*. With water consecrated by this mantra—that is, with water sprinkled over it—if the body of one who has been bitten trembles, that person whose body has thus trembled lives. Alternatively, by another means, through the opening of the eyes, one who has been bitten lives.

‘Not otherwise bitten’: it should be understood that if, upon being sprinkled with that water, a person who has been bitten does not experience trembling of the limbs or twitching of the eyes, then that bitten person shall not survive. This concludes the section on the summary.
Hereafter, the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is described:
one should place the seed-syllables *kṣipa*, *oṃ*, and *svāhā* on the feet, navel, heart, mouth, and head. %Cf. Yogaratnāvalī 1.39
Resembling yellow, white, golden, and black rainbows, respectively.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“‘Cast the seeds, oṃ svāhā’: ‘cast, oṃ svāhā’ refers to the five seed-syllables. ‘One should deposit’ means one should specifically place them. Where? ‘In the feet, navel, heart, mouth, and head’: in these five locations, namely, the two feet, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the crown of the head.”

Of what nature are the seeds? They are “resembling yellow, white, golden, black, and the beautiful bow”: *pīta* means resembling turmeric; *śveta* means white in color; *kāñcana* means golden in color; *asita* means black in color; and *suracāpa* means having the color of Indra’s bow (a rainbow); *nibhāni* means similar to these.

In this manner, one should place the five-colored seed-syllables in sequence: the yellow-colored seed-syllable *kṣi* on the two feet; the white-colored seed-syllable *pa* at the navel; the gold-colored seed-syllable *oṃ* at the heart; the black-colored seed-syllable *svā* in the mouth; and the seed-syllable *hā*, colored like a rainbow, on the crown of the head. Thus is the procedure for the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the limbs.
Hereafter, the method of protection is described:
A four-petalled lotus, joined with the name ending in *bhūta*, with the remaining elements on the petals and surrounded by *māyā*. (10.6) cf. *Yogaratnāvalī* 1.31.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“*Padmaṃ*” means a lotus. “*Caturdalopetaṃ*” means endowed with four petals. “*Bhūtāntaṃ*” refers to the end of the elements—namely those known as earth, water, fire, air, and space; among these, space is the letter *ha*. One should place that letter *ha* in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*). In what manner? “*Nāmasaṃyutaṃ*,” meaning having the name of the victim inserted within it. “*Daleṣu*” means on the four petals situated on the outside. One should write the four seed-syllables of the remaining elements: *kṣipa*, *oṃ*, *svā*, and *hā*.

Having written [the syllable] encircled by *māyā* (the letter *i*), and having written it upon that lotus encircled three times by the syllable *hrīṃ*, one should bind it around the neck of the bitten person; or else, one should draw this *yantra* with sandalwood paste on the chest of the bitten person. Thus is the ritual for protection.
Now the performance of *stobha* is commenced: one should apply the pair "dah-paca" at the end of fire, water, earth, wind, and space.
The *stobha* consisting of the pair "stobhaya" arises from the movement of the central channel (*madhyamikā*). (10.7)
*Vivaraṇa*:

‘Fire’ is the syllable *oṃ*; ‘water’ is the syllable *pa*; ‘earth’ is the syllable *kṣi*; ‘wind’ is the syllable *svā*; ‘space’ is the syllable *ha*. ‘In front’ means at the beginning of these five seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*). ‘The pair *daha-paca* should be joined’: the two words *daha daha* should be joined, and after those, the two words *paca paca* should be joined. ‘The pair *stobhaya*’ refers to the two words *stobhaya stobhaya*. ‘*Stobha*’ means the seizing [of the victim] by the recitation of this mantra.
How so? "From the movement of the middle finger" means from the movement of the middle digit; "it occurs" means it is produced.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ pakṣi svāhā! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Paralyze, paralyze! Thus is the mantra for paralyzing.
Thus ends the procedure for the rite of praise.
Now the neutralization of poison is proclaimed:
the seed-syllable of the Earth (laṃ) should be placed at the beginning and the end, with Water, Fire, and Air (va, ra, ya) joined in the middle;
by the movement of the thumb of the left hand, the pair "stambhaya" constitutes the neutralization. 10.8.
Vivaraṇa:

“The seed-syllable of the earth at the beginning and end” means the seed-syllable of the earth—*kṣi*—at the beginning of the mantra and at the end of the mantra. “The water, fire, and wind should be joined in the middle” means that the three seed-syllables *pa*, *oṃ*, and *sva* should be joined in the middle of the mantra. “The pair *stambhaya*” means the two words *stambhaya* placed after that. “Stambhaḥ” (paralysis): by the recitation of this stated mantra, the spreading of poison is paralyzed. How? “By the movement of the thumb of the left hand,” that is, by moving the thumb of one’s own left hand.
The extraction of the mantra: *Kṣipa oṃ svā kṣi stambhaya stambhaya*. This is the mantra for paralyzing poison.
Now the neutralization of poison is described:
By means of water, earth, fire, air, and space, joined with the two [syllables] *sam* and *plāva*, the removal of poison occurs without delay through the movement of the index finger. 10.9.
*Vivaraṇa*:

‘Water’ is the syllable *pa*; ‘earth’ is the syllable *kṣi*; ‘fire’ is the syllable *oṃ*; ‘wind’ is the syllable *svā*; ‘sky’ is the syllable *hā*. Thus, by means of these five seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*). Of what nature are they?
