They are “endowed with the two [words] causing immersion,” that is, accompanied by the two words *samplāvaya* and *samplāvaya*. What comes about? It certainly occurs. What is it? The “removal of poison,” that is, the rendering of poison non-toxic. From what? “From the movement of the index finger,” that is, from the movement of the index finger of one’s own left hand.
How so? "Acirāt" means quickly. Therefore, the extraction of the mantra is as follows: *Pakṣi oṃ svāhā samplāvaya samplāvaya*. This is the removal of poison.
Now, the curiosity regarding the transference of poison elsewhere is described:

when the two [breaths] moving through the sequence of the stations of wind, fire, water, earth, and space are thoroughly transferred by means of the movement of the ring finger, the transference of poison occurs completely. (10.10)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Marut’ is the syllable *svā*; ‘Agni’ is the syllable *oṃ*; ‘Vāri’ is the syllable *pa*; ‘Dhāma’ is the syllable *kṣi*; ‘Vyoma’ is the syllable *hā*. ‘The pair of steps for transference’ refers to the two words *saṃkrama* and *vraja*. ‘By the movement of the ring finger’ means by the movement of one’s own left ring finger. ‘Completely’ means to an exceeding degree. ‘The transference of poison occurs’ means that the transference of poison takes place toward another.
*Oṃ svā pakṣi hā saṃkrama saṃkrama vraja vraja iti*—this is the mantra for the transference of poison.
The Nāgāveśa (the possession by the serpent-gods):
Through the mantra joined with space, water, fire, wind, and earth, there arises possession;
by reciting "saṃ kṣi pa haḥ pa kṣi pa haḥ" while moving the little finger. (10.11)

Vivaraṇa: ‘Vyoma’ is the syllable *ha*; ‘jala’ is the syllable *pa*; ‘vahni’ is the syllable *oṃ*; ‘pavana’ is the syllable *svā*; ‘kṣiti’ is the syllable *kṣi*. ‘From the joined mantra’ means from the mantra thus combined. ‘It comes to be’ means it is produced from this aforementioned mantra. ‘Then’ (*atha*) means afterwards. ‘Possession’ (*āveśaḥ*) refers to the entry of the Nāga into the human body. It is: *saṃ kṣi pa haḥ pa kṣi pa haḥ*. ‘By reciting’ means by the recitation of this mantra. Why? ‘By moving the little finger,’ that is, by moving the little finger of the left hand.
The extraction of the mantra: hā pa oṃ svākṣi saṃ kṣi pa haḥ pa kṣi pa haḥ. This is the mantra for the possession by a nāga, consisting of these words.
By the whispered recitation of the Bheruṇḍā mantra, one renders a man free from poison;
and by the sprinkling of water, even the Suvarṇarekhā lore neutralizes the effects of being bitten.
Commentary:

"By whispering into the ear" (*karṇajāpyena*) means by whispering into the ear of the person who has been bitten. "Bheruṇḍā" refers to the *vidyā* of the goddess Bheruṇḍā. "It renders poisonless" (*nirviṣaṃ kurute*) means it performs the act of neutralizing poison. "The person" (*naram*) refers to the bitten man. "Even the *Suvarṇarekhā* *vidyā*"—the word "even" (*api*) follows; it is the *Suvarṇarekhā* *vidyā*. "The bitten person"—by the sprinkling of water (*toyābhiṣekataḥ*), that is, by the sprinkling of water consecrated with the *Suvarṇarekhā* *vidyā*, one renders him poisonless.

The extraction of the *bheruṇḍa* spell-mantra: *Oṃ ekahi ekamāte bheruṇḍā vijjābhavikajakaraṇḍe taṃtu maṃtu āmosaï huṃkāra viṣa nāsaï thāvara jaṃgama kittima aṃgaja oṃ phaṭ*. This *bheruṇḍa* spell is to be whispered into the ear; it is a mantra in the Prākṛta language.
Therefore, the extraction of the Suvarṇarekhā mantra: oṃ suvarṇarekhe! kukkuṭavigraharūpiṇi! svāhā // This is the *vidyā* of Suvarṇarekhā for performing the water-consecration (*toyābhiṣeka*).
Having consecrated the water in the jar with the syllable-mantra of earth, water, air, and space, [one should proceed].
From the falling of the stream [of breath] as prescribed for the feet and other locations, there occurs the destruction of poison. || 10.13 ||
*Vivaraṇa*:

‘Bhū’ is *kṣi*; ‘jalaṃ’ is *pa*; ‘marut’ is *svā*; ‘nabho ’kṣaraṃ’ is *hā*. By means of the mantra consisting of these four syllables—namely, *kṣi pa svā hā*—having “consecrated the water in the jar,” that is, having empowered the water in the vessel with this mantra; “by causing the stream to fall starting from the feet,” that is, by pouring down a stream of water beginning from the feet and extending to the head and so forth; “it becomes,” it shall be; “the destruction of poison,” the destruction of the poison of one who has been bitten. The extraction of the mantra is: *kṣipa svāhā*. Thus ends the mantra for the removal of poison.
Now the enumeration of the eight types of nāgas is stated:
Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, the one named Padma, the one called Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and likewise Kuli. (10.14)

Vivaraṇa: ‘Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka’ refers to the nāga named Ananta, the nāga named Vāsuki, and the nāga named Takṣaka. ‘Karkoṭa’ refers to the nāga named Karkoṭaka. ‘Designated as Padma’ refers to the nāga named Padma. ‘And named Mahāsaroja’ refers to the nāga named Mahāpadma. ‘Śaṅkhapāla’ refers to the nāga named Śaṅkhapāla. ‘Likewise Kuli’ refers to the nāga named Kulika. Thus, the names of the eight kinds of nāgas have been specified.
Hereafter, the lineages, species, colors, and manifestations of the poison of those nāgas are described individually:
Vāsuki and Śaṅkha, born of the Kṣatriya lineage, are earth-poisoners and red in color; Karkoṭaka and Padma, who belong to the Śūdra caste, are black and possess the poison of Varuṇī. (10.15)
Commentary:

"Born in a kṣatriya family" means those originating from a kṣatriya lineage. Who are they? Vāsuki and Śaṅkha—the two nāgas Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla. "Earth-poisonous" means those two are endowed with the poison of the earth. "Red" means they are red in color. "Karkoṭaka and Padma as well"—the word "api" (as well) follows after Karkoṭaka and Padma. "Śūdras" means born in a śūdra family. "Black" means those two are black in color. The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. "Vāruṇī-poisonous" means those two are endowed with the poison of the ocean.
The two Brahmins Ananta and Kulika are dark as fire and resemble the moonstone;
Takṣaka and Mahāsarpa are Vaiśyas and are yellow; Marut and Garala are likewise yellow.
Vivaraṇa:

“Anantakulikau” refers to the two nāgas named Ananta and Kulika; “viprau” means those born of the brahmin caste; “vahnigarau” means those possessed of fire-poison; “candrakāntasaṃkāśau” means those resembling the color of crystal; “takṣakamahāsarojau” refers to the two nāgas named Takṣaka and Mahāpadma; “vaiśyau” means those originating from the vaiśya caste; “pītau” means yellow-colored; and “marudgaralau” means those possessed of wind-poison. Thus, the manifestations of the lineage, color, and poison of the eight types of nāgas have been set forth.
In this text, it is not established that the two nāgas Jayavijaya, born from the lineage of the gods, are venomous serpents who do not roam upon the earth.
Now the fourfold symptom is described:
66] by means of a terrestrial poison, there is heaviness, rigidity of the body, and a state of derangement of the humors (saṃnipāta).
The obstruction of the throat by saliva and the trickling [of fluid] from the bite result from water-poisoning.
Vivaraṇa:

"By the earth-poison" means by one bitten by a snake whose poison is of the earth-nature. "Heaviness" is the state of being heavy. "Inertness of the body" is the numbness of the physical frame. "The state of *saṃnipāta*" refers to the nature of a *saṃnipāta* (a combined derangement of the humors); such would be the symptom of earth-poison. "Salivation and constriction of the throat" is the flow of saliva from the mouth. "Oozing of the bite" is the discharge of blood from the spot where the snake has bitten. Why? "From water-poison," that is, from the poison of water; for one bitten by a water-poisonous [creature], such a symptom would occur.

From the defect of fire or poison, there occurs the appearance of swellings and a lack of clarity in vision; from the defect of wind or poison, there occurs a loss of luster and dryness of the mouth. (10.18)
*Vivaraṇa*:

"The appearance of swellings" (*gaṇḍodgamatā*) means the emergence of swellings on the body bitten [by the snake]. "Impairment of vision" (*dṛṣṭer apāṭavam*) means lack of clarity in the eyes. "Occurs" (*bhavati*) means it may happen. Why? "Due to the defect of fiery poison" (*vahniviṣadoṣāt*); such a sign would belong to a person bitten by a snake whose poison is of the fire-nature. "Lack of luster" (*vicchāyatā*) means a bad complexion of the body, and "dryness of the mouth" (*āsyaśoṣaṇam*) also means the absence of moisture in the face. By what? "By the defect of windy poison" (*mārutagaraladoṣeṇa*), that is, by the defect of poison belonging to the wind-nature. Such a sign would belong to a person bitten by a snake whose poison is of the wind-nature.
Thus, the manifestations of the families, colors, poisons, and signs of the eight types of nāgas have been explained.
Having recited the *oṃ namo bhagavatyai* mantra one hundred and eight times, one should strike a drum at a distance of one *krośa* in the vicinity of the victim. 10.19.
Vivaraṇa:

“*Oṃ namo bhagavatyādimantram*” refers to the mantra to be recited hereafter, beginning with “*oṃ namo bhagavati*. “*Aṣṭottaraṃ śatam*” means one hundred and eight. “*Paṭhitvā*” means having performed the recitation. “*Krośapaṭaham*” means a *ḍamaru* drum that resounds for a *krośa*. “*Tāḍayet*” means one should strike it. “*Daṣṭasaṃnidhau*” means in the vicinity of the person who has been bitten.

The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ namo bhagavati vṛddhagaruḍāya sarvaviṣavināśini chinda chinda bhinda bhinda gṛhṇa gṛhṇa ehi ehi bhagavati vidye hara hara huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for the beating of the drum and the proclamation at the ear of one who has been bitten.
Having formed the half-moon mudrā and standing on the right side of the one bitten by the snake, let him say: "Your cow has now been carried off by the bandits. (10.20)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Having assumed the half-moon mudrā” means having assumed the mudrā shaped like a half-moon with the thumb and index finger of the left hand. Where? “On the right side,” that is, in the southern direction. Of whom? “Of the one bitten by a snake,” a man bitten by a serpent. “Having stood,” meaning having remained there. “Let him speak,” let him utter words. What should he say? “Your cow”—your own cow. “Now,” at this very moment. “By the world of thieves,” by the bandits. “Has been led away,” saying, “It has been taken and carried off.”
When told, "Having crushed him with your foot, go," he runs;
he quickly raises him up—such is the power of the mantra.
Vivaraṇa:

“Having struck him with one’s foot” means that the practitioner strikes that bitten person with his own foot. “When told ‘go! means when told ‘depart. “He runs” means that bitten person performs running. “He quickly makes him rise” means he makes that bitten person rise up instantly. “Such is the power of the mantra” means the majesty of the Bhagavatī’s mantra is of this very kind.
The procedure for reviving one bitten by [a venomous creature] by means of beating a drum at the sound of a *krośa*.
Now the ritual procedure for the mantra that summons the *nāgas* is explained:
through one million recitations (*niyuta-japa*) and a fire offering (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of that amount, the summoning of the hooded serpents is accomplished.
The mantra begins with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with *svāhā*, preceded by the sounds *ciri-ciri*. || 10.22 ||
Vivaraṇa:

“From a hundred-thousand recitations” (*niyutajapāt*) means from one hundred thousand recitations. “He attains perfection” (*saṃsidhyati*) means he obtains complete accomplishment. By what means? “By an offering of a tenth part” (*daśāṃśahomena*), that is, by an oblation of ten thousand [recitations]. “The summoning of the hooded ones” (*phaṇisamākṛṣṭiḥ*) is the summoning of the *nāgas*. “Beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*” means beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word *svāhā*. “The mantra beginning with the sound *ciri-ciri*” refers to the mantra that begins with the words *ciri ciri*.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ ciri ciri indravāruṇi ehi ehi kaḍa kaḍa svāhā. This is the mantra for summoning the nāgas.
Now the ritual procedure for the mantra that dispatches the nāgas is declared:

the mantra for dispatching the nāgas is perfected by eighty thousand recitations, followed by a fire-offering (*homa*) of one-tenth that number, and further by the recitation of [offerings] of red oleander flowers (*karavīra*). (10.23)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“The mantra for dispatching the *nāgas*” is the mantra for sending forth the *nāgas* to perform minor rites. “With eighty thousand” means with a measure of eighty thousand. By what? “By recitation. Of what kind? “By an offering of one-tenth,” that is, by an oblation of eight thousand. “Is accomplished” means it attains success (*siddhi*). “Furthermore,” meaning afterwards. Of what [substances]? “Of blood and *karavīra* flowers,” that is, of red *karavīra* flowers.

The extraction of the mantra for dispatching the *nāga*: Oṃ, homage! O *nāga-piśācī*, you with blood-red eyes and a frowning face, whose splendor blazes even from leftovers, come, come, O Blessed One! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā! This is the mantra for dispatching the *nāga*.
One should perform a fire oblation near an anthill, accompanied by the three sweets;
having commanded him for the sake of mantra-perfection, one should dispatch the Lord of Serpents.
Vivaraṇa:

"Near an anthill" means in the vicinity of a termite mound (*vāmalūra*). "Homa" means an oblation. "One should perform" means let him do it. "Endowed with the three sweets" means mixed with milk, clarified butter, and sugar, and provided with flowers previously offered. "Upon the accomplishment of the mantra" means when the accomplishment of the mantra has been achieved through these two types of practice. "Having commanded him" means having issued an order to that Lord of Nagas. "He should dispatch the Lord of Serpents" means he should send forth the Lord of Nagas for the performance of minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*).
The procedure for dispatching the nāgas, performing the ritual service, recitation, and fire offerings has been explained.
"Do not say before anyone, 'I have been sent by him';
do not go with another mantra, nor eat such-and-such a human being. (10.25)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Preṣitaḥ’ means dispatched. Who? ‘I,’ the nāga. By whom? ‘By this’ mantra-practitioner. ‘Thus’ (iti) means in this manner. ‘Do not speak in front of anyone’—do not speak in the presence of any person. ‘Do not go by another mantra’—leaving aside this mantra, do not you go by another mantra. ‘Devour such-and-such a human’—devour that specific person who has been bitten. This is the procedure for dispatching the nāga.
Now the procedure for the descent of the messenger is described:
having extracted the poison from the body of one bitten by a serpent by means of the mantra *oṃ svāhā*, [one should proceed].
One should cause the messenger to fall from the forehead with the mantra, "Somaṃ śrava. || 10.26 ||
*Vivaraṇa*:

“From the body of one bitten by a fanged creature” means from the body of a person bitten by a snake. “By the mantra *oṃ svāhā*” refers to the mantra *oṃ svāhā* which is about to be recited. “Poison” means the poison residing in the body of the bitten person. “Having taken” means having extracted it. How? “Flowing as soma,” that is, flowing as nectar (*amṛta*). From where? “From the forehead,” that is, from the region of the brow. “The messenger” means the one who is sent. “One should cause to fall by means of the mantra”; it should be made to descend.

This is the extraction of the mantras: by means of this mantra, *oṃ svāhā*, poison is drawn out. *oṃ namo bhagavate vajratuṇḍāya svāhā raktākṣi kunakhi dūtaṃ pātaya pātaya mara mara dhara dhara ṭha ṭha ṭha huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe*. This is the mantra for causing the messenger [of death] to fall. *oṃ lām oṃ phaṭ*: by the recitation of this mantra, one bitten by a serpent falls [to the ground]. *oṃ homādiphaḍanta*: this is the mantra for covering the cloth [over the mouth] of the one who has been bitten. (10.27)
Vivaraṇa:

“By the recitation of the mantra ‘oṃ lām oṃ phaṭ,’ by this recitation of the mantra, [the person] falls to the ground. Who? ‘The one bitten by a serpent,’ that is, a man bitten by a snake. ‘Beginning with oṃ homa and ending with phaṭ’ refers to the mantra to be described hereafter, beginning with the word ‘oṃ svāhā’ and ending with the word ‘phaṭ. ‘The mantra for covering the bitten cloth’ is the mantra for covering the body of the fallen, bitten man with a cloth.”

The extraction of the mantras: *Oṃ lāṃ oṃ phaṭ*—this is the mantra for causing the falling of the bitten [victim]. *Oṃ svāhā ru ru ru ru ho plaṃ sarvaṃ hāraya saṃhāraya oṃ ryūṃ oṃ oṃ garuḍākṣi oṃ phaṭ*—this is the mantra for covering the cloth over the bitten [victim].
Having drawn the wind and the sky with the *akṣara-mantra*, he then runs after the cloth;
he runs after it on its back, and wherever the cloth falls, there he [arrives].

"By the syllable-mantra 'apavananabhaḥ' and by the syllable-mantra 'svāhā'; "having drawn [it]," having drawn the cloth that covered the bite; "he runs," he performs the act of running. "From that," from that [mantra]; "the cloth," the covering cloth. "He runs after its back": the person who runs, having pulled that cloth, runs after the back of that bitten one.

"Wherever the cloth falls, there he [is]" means that at the very spot where the cloth held by him falls, right there the bitten person falls. "Svāhā" is the mantra for pulling back the cloth that covered the bitten person.
By this mantra, when whispered softly, the serpent becomes freed from poison;
it departs from its own place, and even if it has been consumed, the poison does not spread. (10.29)

Vivaraṇa: “By this mantra” means by the mantra that has been stated. “The serpent becomes freed from poison” means the snake becomes free of venom. By what means? “By its being uttered,” that is, by the recitation of the mantra to be described. “Gently” means even slowly. “It removes [the poison] from its own place” means that the removal of the poison occurs from the location where the victim was bitten. “Even if [the victim] has eaten it, the poison does not spread” means that even if the person has been swallowed by the snake, no transmission of poison occurs for that person; such is the method of detoxification.

The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tīrthaṃkara Pārśva! Haṃsa! Mahāhaṃsa! Padmahaṃsa! Śivahaṃsa! Kopahaṃsa! Urageśahaṃsa! O Bird, consumer of great poison! Huṃ Phaṭ! Thus ends the mantra for the neutralization of poison.
As he recites the mantra beginning with "Tejo nāma sahasram," the serpent follows behind him; when told, "Go," it turns back.
Vivaraṇa:

"For one reciting the mantra *oṃ namaḥ sahasrādi* (beginning with *oṃ namaḥ sahasrajihve*, etc.), 'the serpent' (*phaṇī*)—meaning a snake—'follows behind him,' that is, follows behind the person who has recited that mantra. 'When told, "Go," he turns back': that very same snake, when told again, "Go," turns around and departs."

The extraction of its mantra is as follows: Oṃ, homage to the thousand-tongued one, the consumer of white lotuses, the long-haired one, the eater of leftovers, svāhā! This is the mantra for the arrival of the Nāgasaha.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gloṃ huṃ kṣūṃ: by means of these two [syllables] ending in *ṭa*, there is the paralysis of the mouths of serpents.
Huṃ kṣūṃ ṭhaṭha: with this, one fixes the gaze during movement; hāṃ kṣāṃ ṭhaṭha: with this, one binds [the gaze]. || 10.31 ||
Vivaraṇa:

“Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gloṃ huṃ kṣūṃ. By means of the mantra “ṭha ṭha,” which consists of two [consonants] ending in *ṭ* (i.e., *ṭha*), there is the “paralysing of the serpent’s mouth” (*phaṇimukhastambha*). By this mantra, the paralysis of the serpent’s mouth occurs. For “the paralysing of movement” (*gamane*), [one uses] “huṃ kṣūṃ ṭha ṭha”; by this mantra, the paralysis of the serpent’s gait occurs. “One binds the gaze” (*dṛṣṭiṃ badhnāti*) with “hāṃ kṣāṃ ṭha ṭha”; one binds the serpent’s gaze with the mantra “hāṃ kṣāṃ ṭha ṭha.”
Thus ends the procedure for paralyzing the movement and vision of the serpent’s mouth.
The Garuḍa commands Vāma Suvarṇarekhā:
therefore, having uttered the mantra ending in *svāhā*, perform the coiling.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“‘Of Suvarṇarekhā’ refers to the word *suvarṇarekhāyāḥ*. ‘Garuḍa commands from here’ means that after the word *suvarṇarekhā*, the phrase *garuḍājñāpayati* follows. ‘Having uttered the mantra ending in *svāhā*’ means having recited that mantra with the word *svāhā* at its conclusion. ‘Perform the coiling’ [is the command].
The extraction of the mantra is as follows: *oṃ suvarṇarekhāyā garuḍājñāpayati kuṇḍalīkaraṇaṃ kuru kuru svāhā*.”
Accompanied by the *praṇava*, ending with *svāhā*, and joined with "lalalalalala," this mantra causes even the Lord of the Nāgas to enter a jar in an instant. (10.33)

Vivaraṇa: "Accompanied by the *praṇava*" means beginning with the syllable *oṃ*; "ending with *svāhā*" means having the word *svāhā* at its conclusion. "Joined with *la-la-la-la-la-la*" means endowed with the six syllables *la-la-la-la-la-la*. "It performs" means it effects. "This mantra" refers to the mantra just described. What does it perform? "The entry into the jar," that is, the entry into the vessel. "In an instant" means in a mere moment. Of whom? "Even of the Lord of the Nāgas," that is, even of the sovereign of the serpents; in an instant, it effects the entry into the jar even for him.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ la-la-la-la-la-la svāhā. This is the mantra for entering the jar of the hooded serpent.

"Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, by the command of Garuḍa, ṭhaṭha!"—by means of this mantra and the corresponding mudrā, a line is drawn which a serpent can never, under any circumstances, cross, even when at the point of death. (10.34)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“With the mantra *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ garuḍājñā ṭhaṭha*,” means by means of this mantra. “With that mudrā,” means with the Garuḍa-mudrā. “The line drawn,” means the line drawn on the ground by the practitioner. “The serpent in a state of death,” means the snake having reached the state of death. “Does not cross over,” means it is unable to leap across. “At any time whatsoever,” means at any point in time.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ garuḍāya ṭha ṭha. This is the mantra for the lines.
Having empowered chalk with *kapikacchū* and *rasa*, and having consecrated it with the *praṇava* and other mantras,
one should draw a chalk-snake according to the instruction on Saturday.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Chalk infused with *kapikacchū* juice” means chalk that has been infused seven times with the juice of *kaṇḍukarī*. “Having recited over it with the *praṇava* and the blue [mantra]” means having recited that chalk together with the *praṇava* and the blue mantra. “It is to be drawn with that” means it is to be written with that chalk. How? “According to the instruction,” preceded by the oral instruction. What is it? “The chalk-snake,” the snake drawn with that chalk. Where? “On a Saturday,” on the day of Saturn.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ nīlaviṣamahāviṣasarpasaṃkrāmaṇi svāhā. This is the mantra for transferring poison.
Whoever should strike that face, a chalk-snake bites him; of this there is no doubt.
Upon seeing the bite-mark upon the palm of his hand, he faints, overwhelmed by the agony of the poison. (10.36)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Whoever would strike that face, a chalk-snake bites him; there is no doubt in this. Here, one should not entertain any doubt regarding the procedure for the chalk-snake. “Having seen the bite on the palm”: having seen the mark of that snake’s bite upon the palm. “He faints”: the person undergoes a loss of consciousness. Of what nature is he? “Agitated by the pain of poison”: agitated by the pain produced by the poison. Thus ends the procedure for the curious rite of the chalk-snake.
Hereafter, the procedure for the root-poison is described:

having recited the mantra "oṃ kroṃ proṃ trīṃ ṭhaḥ" while the poison is situated within the syllable *hrūṃ*, one should gaze at the sun with one's eyes and then consume it by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). (10.37)
Vivaraṇa:

By means of this mantra, “Oṃ kroṃ proṃ trīṃ ṭhaḥ,” [one acts]. “Poison” refers to stationary poison (*sthāvaraviṣa*). Of what nature is it? It is said that the poison is situated in the middle of the syllable *hrūṃ* within the palm of the hand. Having “recited” it—that is, having empowered it with the mantra—one should “look at the sun,” meaning one should gaze at the sun with one’s vision. One should then “consume” it, i.e., perform the act of consuming the poison. How? “From the inhalation (*pūraka*),” that is, by means of the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*).
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ kroṃ proṃ trīṃ ṭhaḥ. This is the mantra for consuming poison.
Having meditated upon the poison as being like something blue, it should be given for the sake of an antidote;
then, the reciter of the mantra should recite "glauṃ hlauṃ" and thereafter "ghe ghe."
Vivaraṇa:

“To the adversary” means for the world of enemies. “Should be given” means it must be bestowed. “Having meditated” means having performed meditation. Of what nature? “Blue-hued,” meaning its essential form is blue in color. What is it? “Poison,” namely root-poison. Having done what? “Having consecrated with the mantra *glauṃ hlauṃ*,” meaning having empowered it with this mantra. “But” (*tu*) means furthermore. “From that” (*tataḥ*), meaning from the two seed-syllables *glauṃ* and *hlauṃ*. “*Ghe ghe*,” meaning having recited the word *ghe ghe*. By whom? “By the practitioner” (*mantriṇā*), that is, by the one who utters the mantra.
The extraction of the mantra: *glauṃ hlauṃ ghe ghe*. This is the mantra for administering poison to an adversary while visualizing him as blue.

The urine of a female horse, a female elephant, and a female donkey, along with bitter gourd, a virgin girl, the three pungents, *kuṣṭha*, and *indrayava*, destroy poison when administered as a nasal drop or by drinking. (10.39)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Muni’ is Agasti; ‘Hayagandhā’ is Aśvagandhā; ‘Ghoṣā’ is Devadālī; ‘Vandhyā’ is Karkoṭī; ‘Kaṭutumbikā’ is Kaṭukālābukā; ‘Kumārī’ is Gṛhakanyā; ‘Trikaṭuka’ is Tryūṣaṇa; ‘Kuṣṭha’ is Ruk; ‘Indrayavā’ is the seed of Kuṭaja. They ‘destroy,’ that is, they eliminate. ‘Poison,’ meaning both stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama) poison. How? ‘By snuffing and drinking’: by the administration of these medicines as nasal drops (nasya) and by drinking them, all poison is destroyed.

A parasol made from the skin of a two-humped camel, combined with the milk of a sun-anointed *śleṣmataru* tree and the fruit of that same tree, effects the transfer of scorpion venom through contact with a staff made from a *badarī* tree. 10.40.
Vivaraṇa:

“A parasol arisen from two pure elephants” means a parasol produced from two pure elephants. “Melted sun” means the milk of the sun (*mārtaṇḍa*). “Endowed with the fruit of the *śleṣmataru* tree” means accompanied by the pulp of the *śleṣmātaka* fruit. “The transfer of scorpion venom” means the removal of scorpion venom and the transfer of other poisons.

“From the conjunction of the jujube fruit and the staff”: on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, having taken a jujube thorn possessing two spikes—one pointing upward and one pointing downward—and having applied the paste of those three medicinal substances, one transfers [the poison] from the upward-pointing spike to the downward-pointing spike, and thus it is transferred from one to the other.
Whoever writes the vidyā of Kurukullā within a hexagonal house in their home, no nāga remains there once it has been written with the binding of the nāga-enemy. 10.41.
Vivaraṇa:

"In the middle of a hexagonal abode" means in the center of a hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*). "Kurukullā" refers to the mantra of the goddess named Kurukullā. "Whoever should write" means whichever practitioner of mantra (*mantravādī*) should write. Where? "In the house," that is, on the threshold of the house, on the upper part of its entrance. What? "The lore" (*vidyā*), namely the lore of the goddess Kurukullā. "There," in that house, "it does not stay. What does not stay? "The nāga," meaning a serpent. Under what condition? "When it has been written.
By whom? "By the binding of the enemy of nāgas," that is, by the binding of Garuḍa.
The mantra: oṃ kurukulle hūṃ phaṭ.
Now the drawing out of the mandala is described:
having drawn a most beautiful square mandala with powder of five colors, one should place water-filled jars in the four corners. (10.42)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Square” means perfectly square. “Maṇḍala” refers to the maṇḍala that is about to be described. “Exceedingly beautiful” means shining with extreme splendor. “With five-colored powder” means with powder of five colors—namely, white, red, yellow, green, and black. “Having drawn” means having drawn it with excellence. “In the four corners” means in the four corners of that maṇḍala. “Filled with water” means completely filled with water. One should place them. Which ones? “Flasks,” that is, jars.
Above that was a much more spacious pavilion, strewn with garlands of exceedingly fragrant flowers, and provided with moonstones, banners, arches, the sound of bells, and mirrors. (10.43)
Vivaraṇa:

‘Upon that’ means upon that maṇḍala. ‘Vipulataraṃ’ means extremely extensive. ‘Maṇḍapaṃ’: of what nature is it? ‘Strewn with garlands of exceedingly fragrant flowers. Again, of what nature is it? ‘Endowed with moon-crests, banners, archways, the sound of bells, and mirrors’—that is, it is provided with canopies, banners, wreaths for salutation, small bells, and distinguished mirrors.
One should write the five *parameṣṭhi* mantras, each preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *homānta*,
in the center of an eight-petaled lotus using camphor, saffron, and sandalwood. (10.44)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“The *pañcaparameṣṭhimantra* is the mantra of the Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, Upādhyāyas, and all Sādhus. And how is this [mantra] characterized? It is ‘each individually,’ meaning separately for each. It is ‘preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with the *homānta*,” that is, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word *svāhā*. ‘In the middle of an eight-petaled lotus’ means in the center of an eight-petaled water-lily, specifically within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the eight-petaled [lotus]. ‘With camphor, saffron, and sandalwood’ means with *karpūra*, *kāśmīra*, and *śrīgandha*. ‘One should write’ means one should write it specifically.”

The extraction of the mantras: Oṃ arhadbhyaḥ svāhā, Oṃ siddhebhyaḥ svāhā, Oṃ sūribhyaḥ svāhā, Oṃ pāṭhakebhyaḥ svāhā, Oṃ sarvasādhubhyaḥ svāhā. Thus, one should write the mantra of the five supreme beings (pañcaparameṣṭhin) in the center of the pericarp.
One should offer oblations to these deities, Jayā and the others, as well as Jambhā and the others, in the eastern fire and the subsequent directions;
then, in the southern quarter of that, [one should place] the golden sandal of the Goddess.
Vivaraṇa:

"In the east, fire, and so forth" means in the four cardinal directions beginning with the east, and in the four intermediate directions beginning with the southeast. "Clearly" (hi) means evidently. "These" refers to the deities previously mentioned. "On its southern side" means in the region of the southern direction of that mandala. "Made of gold" means fashioned from gold. "The sandals of the Goddess" means one should offer a pair of sandals to the Goddess.

The sequence of installation: 1. *Oṃ jaye svāhā* in the eastern direction; 2. *Oṃ vijaye svāhā* in the southern direction; 3. *Oṃ ajite svāhā* in the western direction; 4. *Oṃ aparājite svāhā* in the northern direction; 5. *Oṃ jambhe svāhā* in the south-eastern direction; 6. *Oṃ mohe svāhā* in the south-western direction; 7. *Oṃ stambhe svāhā* in the north-western direction; 8. *Oṃ stambhini svāhā* in the north-eastern direction. Thus, one should inscribe the deities beginning with Jaya and ending with Jambha upon the eight petals.
Having worshipped with perfumes, rice grains, flowers, food offerings, lamps, incense, and fruits,
one should [worship] the Parameṣṭhin mantra and the feet of Bhairava and Padmāvatī.
Vivaraṇa:

‘Having worshipped’ means having performed adoration. With what? ‘With perfumes, rice, flowers, food offerings, lamps, incense, and fruits’—that is, with the eightfold materials of worship consisting of auspicious sandalwood paste, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flowers, cooked rice as an offering, lamps, incense, fruits, and so forth. ‘And the mantra of the Supreme Beings’ refers to the mantra of the five *parameṣṭhins*. ‘Having worshipped’ means having honored it. ‘One should worship the feet of Bhairava and Padmāvatī’ means one should also worship the feet of the deities Bhairava and the goddess Padmāvatī, which are their golden sandals.

A disciple who is detached from the people of other systems, devoted to the Jina’s system, the deity, and the guru, having been provided with garments and ornaments and having bathed, [should be seated] facing the mandala. (10.47)
Vivaraṇa:

“Detached from the people of other systems” means detached from the world of false teachings. “The disciple” refers to the one to be trained. Furthermore, of what nature is he? “Devoted to the Jina’s system, the deity, and the guru” means devoted to the Jina’s doctrine, the deity, and the true guru. “Having prepared his garments and ornaments” means one by whom the garments and ornaments have been prepared; him, thus prepared. Furthermore, of what nature is he? “Well-bathed” means properly bathed. “Facing the maṇḍala” means facing the maṇḍala that has been drawn out.
Having bathed him with four jars containing gold, and having given him other garments and such,
he should then impart to him the mantra received from the lineage of gurus.
*Vivaraṇa*:

“Having bathed him” means having properly bathed that disciple. With what? “With four jars,” namely, the four full jars situated in the corners of the previously prepared maṇḍala. Of what nature are they? “With gold,” meaning accompanied by gold. “Him” refers to the disciple. “Then,” immediately after the bathing. “Having given other garments and so forth,” meaning having removed the previous garments and the like, and having given other new garments and so forth. “To him,” to such a disciple, “he should impart the mantra.”
Of what nature is the mantra? It is "arrived from the lineage of gurus," meaning it has come down through the succession of teachers.
We have bestowed upon you this mantra, which has come down through the lineage of gurus,
having made the fire, the sun, the moon, the stars, the sky, and the multitude of mountains our witnesses.
Vivaraṇa:

"To you" means to you, the disciple. "Given by us. "This mantra" refers to the mantra previously mentioned. Of what nature is it? "Transmitted through the lineage of gurus," meaning it has come down by way of the succession of teachers. Having done what? "Having made witnesses," that is, having made them bear witness. Which ones? "The hosts of fire, sun, moon, stars, sky, and mountains"—the multitudes of fire, sun, moon, constellations, space, and mountains.

Even you must not give it to a person devoid of right view; rather, [it should be given] to one who possesses devotion toward the guru, the deity, and the observances, and who is endowed with virtuous qualities.
Vivaraṇa:

“By you also” means even by yourself. “It should not be given” means it must not be bestowed. To whom? “To one devoid of right view,” that is, to one lacking in *samyaktva*. “To a person” means to a human being. “But rather” (or alternatively): “to one who possesses devotion toward the Guru, the Deity, and the *samaya*,” that is, to one endowed with devotion for the Guru, the Deity, and the tradition; “to one endowed with virtues,” meaning to one joined with all [excellent] qualities—it should be given to a person distinguished by such qualities.
If, out of greed or affection, you should give [the food] to one who observes another rule, that sin which comes from killing a child, a woman, a cow, or a sage shall be yours. (10.51)
*Vivaraṇa*:

"Out of greed" means out of desire for wealth; or alternatively, "out of affection" means out of delusion. "If you will give" means if you will give this *vidyā*. To whom? "To one devoted to another doctrine," that is, to one possessed of devotion to a rival system. Then, "whatever sin there is in the killing of children, women, cows, and sages"—that is, whatever sin results from the slaughter of children, women, cattle, and sages—"that shall be yours"; that sin shall belong to you. Having made him hear this in the presence of the Guru and the deity:
The preceptor should transmit the mantra through the practice of mantra-attainment.

*Vivaraṇa*: “That” refers to the recipient of the mantra. “Having caused him to hear thus” means having made him take an oath in this manner. How? “In the presence of the guru and the deity,” that is, in the vicinity of the guru and the deity. “The practitioner of mantras” (mantrī) refers to the one who speaks the mantra. “He should offer” means he should entrust [it]. What? “The mantra,” namely, the mantra descended through the lineage of the gurus. How? “Through the application of the mantra’s means of accomplishment” (sādhana), that is, by means of the method for propitiating the mantra.
Praise—
May the venerable Ajitasena Gaṇin, whose pair of feet is set upon the crowns of all kings,
the remover of misfortunes and the deliverer of the multitude of the fortunate from the ocean of existence, be victorious! (10.53)
*Vivaraṇa*:

“He whose pair of lotus-feet is joined by the crowns of all kings” means he whose two lotus-feet are touched by the crowns of all monarchs. “The illustrious Gaṇin Ajitasena” refers to the venerable teacher Ajitasena. “May he be victorious” means may he abide in supreme excellence. “The remover of misfortune” means the remover of sin. Furthermore, of what nature is he? “The one who ferries across the ocean of existence for the multitude of the fortunate” means the savior from the sea of *saṃsāra* for the assembly of those destined for liberation (*bhavya*).
His disciple was Gaṇi Kanakasena, who understood the scriptures of the Jina’s doctrine, who cut down the dense forest of saṃsāra, and who was skilled at burning the fuel of karma. (10.54)

Vivaraṇa: “One who knows the scriptures of the Jina’s doctrine” (*jinasamayāgamavedī*) means one who understands all the scriptures of the doctrine of the Lord of Jinas (*jineśvara*). “The cutter of the dense forest of saṃsāra” (*gurutarasaṃsārakānanocchedī*) means one capable of uprooting the difficult-to-traverse wilderness of worldly existence. “Skilled in burning the fuel of karma” (*karmendhanadahanapaṭuḥ*) means one who is exceedingly expert in the act of burning the fuel of all karmas. “His disciple” (*tacchiṣyaḥ*) means the disciple of the venerable teacher Ajitasena. Who is he? He is Kanakasena Gaṇin, the teacher Kanakasena.

Jinasena became his disciple; his body was adorned with virtuous conduct, he was free from attachment, he had crushed the invincible god of love, and he was like a sun to the lotuses of those capable of liberation. 10.55.
Vivaraṇa:

“One whose limbs are adorned with conduct” means one whose body is adorned with every form of right conduct (*cāritra*). “Detached” (*niḥsaṅga*) means free from external and internal possessions. “One by whom the invincible Anaṅga was crushed”: *anaṅga* (the bodiless one) who is difficult to conquer is *durjayānaṅga*; he by whom that *durjayānaṅga* was crushed is *mathitadurjayānaṅga*, meaning one who has conquered Madana (the god of love). “His disciple” means the disciple of the teacher Kanakasena. Who is he? “Jinasena,” the teacher Jinasena. “He became” means he was born.
Of what nature was he? “The sun for the lotuses of the worthy” (*bhavya*), meaning a sun for the awakening of the lotuses of those destined for liberation.
His disciple was Malliṣeṇa, who obtained the grace of a boon from Sarasvatī;
by him this ritual manual (kalpa) of the deity Bhairava was composed in four hundred verses in summary.

Vivaraṇa: “His disciple” means the disciple of the teacher Jinasena. “Was born” means he came into existence. Who? Malliṣeṇa, that is, the teacher Malliṣeṇa. Of what nature was he? “One who obtained the grace of a boon from Sarasvatī,” meaning he received the favor of a boon from the goddess Sarasvatī. “By him” refers to the teacher Malliṣeṇa. “Expounded” means narrated. “Of the deity Bhairava” refers to the goddess Bhairavapadmāvatī. “The ritual manual (kalpa)” means a collection of mantra-instructions. “In brief” means in a concise manner.
“In four hundred [verses]” means with a textual extent of four hundred verses.
As long as the oceans, mountains, clusters of stars, the sky, the moon, and the sun endure, may this ritual manual (kalpa) of Bhairava and Padmāvatī remain. 10.57
Vivaraṇa:

“As long as” (*yāvat*) means for as long as time lasts. “The ocean” (*vārdhiḥ*) is the sea. “The mountain-bearer” (*mahīdharaḥ*) is a principal mountain range. “The host of stars” (*tārāgaṇaḥ*) is the collection of constellations. “The sky” (*gaganaṃ*) is the atmosphere. “The moon” (*candraḥ*) is the one marked by the deer. “The lord of day” (*dinapatiḥ*) is the sun (*mārtaṇḍa*). As long as these—the ocean and so forth—“remain” (*tiṣṭhanti*), that is, will endure; “for so long” (*tāvat*), for that duration of time, “let it remain” (*āstām*). “The ritual manual of Bhairava-Padmāvatī” (*bhairavapadmāvatīkalpaḥ*) is the ritual manual of the mantra of the goddess named Bhairava-Padmāvatī.
Thus ends the Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa, composed by the venerable Malliṣeṇa Sūri, the crest-jewel of poets in both languages.
